messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I glance up the lane where Hesper is looking, then step inside first, keeping my sword sheathed. I move clear of the doorway so Sefa and Pell can follow.

“Best talk away from the street, then. What needs doing by nightfall—and who are you watching for?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps across the threshold first, unhurried, and gives Hesper a small nod—the kind you give a patient's family when they haven't said the worst of it yet.

"Nightfall, then," she says quietly. "We'll hear it inside, I think. Better than on the step."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell follows her gaze up the lane before he looks at her again. He takes in the main street, the doorways, whoever's idling where they shouldn't be. Then he steps in, out of the sun, and keeps his voice low.

"You looked up that lane like you were expecting someone. Worth knowing who, before we hear the rest." He pauses on the threshold and nods at the closed shutters. "And if it's the sort of someone who watches doors, I'd rather we talk in a room without windows to the street."

Once he's inside, he moves aside so the others can come in. He stays near the door where he can still see the gap.

*(Passive Perception 14 on the lane as I glance up it: anyone loitering, anyone who turns away too quickly?)*

scenes.narration:
Bram looks up the lane before he steps inside, and Pell's eyes follow his a moment later.

It's an ordinary Beregost morning. A coal cart is backing into the smithy yard at the bottom of the lane. At the top, where the lane meets the main street, a horse trough stands by the corner. A stable lad sits on its edge with straw on his sleeves, picking at a heel of bread and watching the carts. Across from him, in the shade of the cooper's doorway, a tiefling in a road-dusty coat leans on the wall. When Pell's look reaches him, he turns away quickly, toward the cooper's shut door, and finds something to study in the planking. The lad doesn't turn at all. He just keeps eating.

Bram goes in first, his sword sheathed, and steps to the left of the doorway. Sefa comes right behind him with her small, unhurried nod. Pell comes last, out of the sun. He stops where he can still see a hand's width of the lane through the gap.

The hall smells of beeswax and cold ashes. Hesper shuts the door, drops the bar, and stands a moment with her palm flat on the oak.

"Someone has stood at the top of the lane three mornings running," she says. "Young, I think. I see him from the upstairs window, and never well. I don't know who he is. I don't know who sends him." She looks at Pell. "You're right about the street. Come through."

She takes them down the hall, past a front room where the furniture sits under dust sheets, to a study at the back. Its one window looks onto a walled yard with a rain barrel and a pear tree. Shelves of bound ledgers cover two walls. A notary's desk sits under the window, tidy and unused, with a rack of seal-stamps and a dish of red wax that has gone dull with dust. Hesper doesn't sit. She stands behind the desk, her inked hand resting on its edge.

"My husband was Aubrey Vallow, notary of this town for twenty years. He died this winter. He fell on the steps of the Song of the Morning." She says it like an entry in a register. "Eight months ago he pledged an iron coffer to a moneylender on the main street, Gaspar Thole. I didn't know until last week, when Thole sent me a courtesy notice as the widow. The term of the pledge ends at sundown today. After that, Thole may sell it, and he has a buyer. A Master Corwen Ashby. I don't know him."

"I have been to Thole twice. The first time he was polite and told me nothing. The second time he didn't open the door."

From a drawer she takes a leather purse and sets it on the desk. It's heavy, and it stays where she put it.

"The terms. I want the coffer brought here, to this room, before sundown. Fifty gold now, a hundred more on delivery. How you get it from Thole is your affair, provided nothing is done that puts my name before the temple court. And one condition, which isn't negotiable." She raises her eyes to each of them in turn. "It comes to me shut. Not opened, not tried, not looked into. Aubrey asked me to keep it shut, and I mean to."

She waits with her hand beside the purse and doesn't push it toward any of them.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I leave the purse where it is.

“Is that fifty our advance, or the money to redeem the pledge? How much does Thole say he's owed—and have you papers showing your right to collect it?”

I glance at the dusty seal-stamps, then back to her.

“I can agree to leave it shut. But before we take your coin: what do you know of what's inside, and has anyone besides your husband warned you against opening it? If there's danger in carrying it, we need to know.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa folds her hands in front of her and makes no move toward the purse.

"We'll take it on. But before that purse changes hands, tell us three things plainly." Her voice is low and even. "Do you have Aubrey's note of pledge—the number of the debt, the surety written? If we walk into Thole's shop with nothing but a widow's word, he can name any sum and shut the door again."

She glances at the closed window and back to Hesper. "And the coffer itself. You said iron. Is it small enough to carry under one arm, or will we need a cart and two strong backs? Has it any mark we can swear to—a scratch, a lockplate, a letter, a way of proving it is your husband's and not some other man's coffer?"

A pause. "And the watcher at the top of the lane. These three mornings—when does he stop? Does he stay after the doors open, or only until someone shows at a window? Thole may not have been as courteous as his notice."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't reach for the purse. He glances back down the hall toward the barred door, then at Hesper.

"Your watcher might have company. There's a tiefling in a road coat in the cooper's doorway, across from the trough. He turned away when I looked at him, quicker than a man with nothing to hide. The stable lad didn't turn at all. So either one of them is yours, or there are two of them." He shrugs. "Worth knowing before we walk out of here carrying anything."

He nods at the shelves of ledgers.

"Here's the part I care about. A pledge has a price to buy it back. What did Aubrey borrow against it, and what does Thole want by sundown? If you can just pay it, the easiest way to get your coffer is to walk in the front door with the money, and nobody goes near a temple court. And a notary of twenty years doesn't pledge anything without writing it down. Did he keep his copy of the contract? The pledge note, a receipt, a ledger entry with Thole's name on it? If that paper's in this room, it's worth more to us than any lockpick."

He leaves a beat, then asks the last question more quietly.

"I won't open it. You have my word, and I keep that one. But I'd like to know what I'm carrying, at least from the outside. How big is it, how heavy, and is there a key? Does Thole have one, or did Aubrey keep it?"

*(If she has no answer on the pledge papers, I'd like to search the ledgers for Thole's name or the pledge date. Investigation +4.)*

cards.title: Investigation: Aubrey's day-books — anything on Thole, the pledge, or where the ticket went

presses.text:
Pell sits at the dead man's desk and runs a finger down the margins, looking for names and figures. He doesn't read every line. Before he turns the first page, he taps the notice where it lies beside the purse.

"Yellow wax on the hasp," he says quietly, without looking up. "And every stamp he owned takes red. Either he borrowed someone else's seal to close it, or the coffer was closed for someone else."

He starts going through the day-books from about eight months back, looking for Thole's name, a hundred and twenty, or any entry in that square hand that's shorter than it ought to be.
presses.reply:
Got it. Pell's paragraph goes into the turn as written: he sits at the desk, says his line about the wax, and works back through the day-books from about eight months ago. The check stands as called: Investigation, DC 15, with his +4. That covers the search itself. It's a dead man's private hand over eight months of entries, and an entry that's been kept short on purpose doesn't jump out, so it isn't routine ledger work.

His remark about the wax is his own reasoning spoken aloud, so it doesn't need a roll. Hesper will answer it, or not, in her own way. What the notice actually shows, and what the books give up, I'll settle against what's already on the table when the die comes back. If any detail in his line (the colour of the wax, the figure) doesn't match what's been established, I'll say so in one plain line outside the story rather than quietly bending it. Roll when you're ready.

Has it any mark we can swear to—a scratch, a lockplate, a letter, a way of proving it is your husband's and not some other man's coffer?" A pause. "And the watcher at the top of the lane. These three mornings—when does he stop? Does he stay after the doors open, or only until someone shows at a window? Thole may not have been as courteous as his notice."

Nobody touches the purse. Hesper looks at it, then at Bram, as though he had asked the right question first.

"The fifty is yours. It's yours whatever Thole asks." She opens the drawer again and lays a folded sheet beside the purse. It has been opened and closed so often it lies flat along its creases. "His notice. Read it."

It's written in a careful moneylender's hand that takes care over the figures. *To the widow of Master Aubrey Vallow.* One coffer of iron, banded, small enough for one man to carry, its hasp sealed in yellow wax, deposited by the said Master Vallow eight months since, against a loan of one hundred and twenty gold pieces. Redeemable until sundown of this day *by the bearer of the ticket, or the lawful heir producing it.* After that it falls forfeit to the undersigned. A buyer, Master Corwen Ashby, has declared his interest. *G. Thole, in his own hand.*

"A hundred and twenty," Hesper says. "If he'll take it lawfully, I'll pay it, and your hundred still stands. I can't go far past that." She answers Bram's other question in the same even tone. "I'm his widow and his heir. The will was proved before the temple court in the spring, and I hold the copy. I showed it to Thole the first time. He read it twice and said the terms stand as written. He wouldn't tell me whether that meant he'd take my money." A pause. "I have no ticket. There's no copy of the pledge in this house. I've been through his papers. It's the only paper I ever knew him not to keep."

She turns to Sefa. "I never saw the coffer. What you've just read is all I know of it." She tips her chin at the rack of stamps and the dish of dull red wax. "Aubrey sealed in red. Every stamp in that rack is his, and every one takes red."

To you: "If there's a key, I haven't found it. The notice doesn't mention one."

Then back to Bram's last question. "I don't know what's in it. Nobody has warned me of anything. That notice is the only word anyone has sent me about it. Pell finds it. Eight months back, between a lease on a malting-house and a will witnessed for a tanner, there's a line with nothing beside it: *G.T. — noon.* Hesper has seen that already; he can tell from the way she doesn't lean in. He reads on, though, back through the winter into the autumn before, and two entries a few weeks apart stop him. They read *Song. Archive. Sr. M.K.*, the same three words twice. Beside the second, in the margin, is something that isn't writing. It's a small inked circle, cut down the middle by an upright stroke that ends in a little hook at the foot, like the bit of a key. Nothing else in either book looks like it.

Hesper looks where his finger rests. "Sister Maudra Kell keeps the temple archive. Aubrey did the temple's leases and bequests for years. I saw those entries." Her eyes move to the margin and stay there. "That mark I don't know. It isn't one of his."

The bell of the Song of the Morning hasn't rung again. Half an hour has gone by since you came in off the lane, and the purse still sits on the desk where she put it.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“What have you found, Pell?”

I step beside the desk to look at the entry and the unfamiliar mark without disturbing the pages.

“Mistress Vallow, we'll try the lawful road first. We'll need that notice, your proved copy of the will, and your written authority to act for you. Keep the redemption money ready until we know whether Thole will accept it without the ticket.”

I glance toward Sefa and Pell. “If he won't, we find out precisely why. Sister Maudra may be able to help us after that.”

Then I turn back to Hesper. “One other thing. Did Aubrey seem hurt or frightened when he told you to keep it shut? And was anyone with him when he fell?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps to the desk without taking the notice from Hesper's side, and bends a little over the open day-book.

"Show me exactly where the margin mark lies," she says to Pell. "The widow says it isn't Aubrey's hand. If it's writing of any kind, I may be able to read it."

She lets her eyes pass from the mark to the entries around it, then looks up at Hesper. "Thole's wording is a leash with two knots. 'The bearer of the ticket' he has never given you, and 'the lawful heir producing it'—producing the ticket, the will, or the coffer? A temple clerk could argue that for a month. We have until sundown, so we won't argue unless we must."

A pause. "His notice says the pledge ended because the ticket is lost. But a notary of twenty years kept a day-book. If Aubrey wrote what was pledged and to whom, and some other hand put a mark beside it, that mark may tell us whether Thole has been here once already to tidy his side of the shelf."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell copies the mark onto a scrap of paper with Aubrey's own pen: the circle, the upright stroke, the little hook at the foot. He blows on it and tucks it inside his coat. Then he finally reaches over and takes the purse, weighs it once in his palm, and sets it down nearer the middle of the desk, where it belongs to all three of them.

"We'll take it." He turns the notice so the others can see one line, and taps it. "*By the bearer of the ticket, or the lawful heir producing it.* That's a moneylender's way of saying the ticket comes first. Aubrey kept every paper he ever touched except this one. So either he hid it, or he gave it to someone. If it's in a stranger's hand by sundown, Thole can hand the coffer over and call it lawful, and your will won't stop him. I'd wager Master Ashby knows where that ticket is, even if we don't."

He looks at Bram and Sefa.

"Here's how I'd cut it. Mistress Vallow goes to Thole with the hundred and twenty and the will, and she doesn't go alone. One of you walks in beside her. He shut his door on a widow. He won't do that to a man in chain mail with a writ in her hand, not in daylight on the main street. If he takes the money, we're done by noon." A pause. "If he won't, I want to know why. And I want to know where Thole keeps things, and whether Ashby has already been in to see it."

He nods toward the front of the house.

"Our watcher leaves before noon. I'd like to see where he goes. I'll slip out the back over the yard wall and pick him up from the corner. The tiefling first, since he's the one who flinched." He holds up the folded scrap. "Then the temple. Sister Kell saw Aubrey twice in her archive, and this mark sits beside the second visit. If it's a temple sign, she'll know it. If it isn't, her face will tell me."

To Hesper, quieter: "Is the yard gate barred, and does it come out on another lane? I'd rather nobody sees four of us leave by your front door."

scenes.narration:
Bram steps up beside the desk. The day-book is open where Pell left it, and the entry is easy to read: *Song. Archive. Sr. M.K.*, with the small inked figure in the margin beside it. It is a circle with one upright stroke through it, hooked at the foot.

Sefa leans in over the page from the other side, close enough to see the strokes of the ink. Her eyes have read every script ever put in front of them. They find nothing to read here: no letter, no glyph, no cipher. It is a drawing of something. The hand that made it went slowly and carefully, the way you copy a thing you have only seen once.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I'll walk with you, Mistress Vallow. Bring the will and the redemption money. We go when you're ready—no sense letting the morning slip.”

I fold the authority and notice carefully into my pack.

“Pell, we'll give you those fifteen minutes to get into place. I won't hail you if I spot you. Mind yourself; we don't yet know that either fellow is watching this house.”

I turn to Sefa. “I'd welcome you beside us at Thole's. Another pair of ears may be worth more than the mail.”

While Hesper gets ready, I loosen my sword belt a notch so the hilt sits comfortably, keeping the blade sheathed. “We're going to offer payment, not threaten him. Let him give us his answer plainly.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes the fifty and counts it out on the desk in three piles: seventeen, seventeen, sixteen. He pushes the two larger ones toward Bram and Sefa and pockets the small one without comment.

"Go now," he tells Hesper. "Don't wait for him to leave. I want him to see you walk down that lane with Bram beside you. If he's only watching the house, he'll stay put. If he's watching for the coffer, he'll run to whoever pays him the moment you turn toward Thole's. Either way, I'll learn something."

He looks at Bram. "Give me a count of a hundred before you open the front door. I'll be in the alley by then. Walk slowly, and don't look at the corner. Let him have a good look at you."

presses.text:
Pell keeps to the ivy side of the alley, where the shade lies deepest. He walks rather than creeps, an ordinary man going about his business behind the smithies, until the bellows boy's eyes are on the coals and the carter has a harness strap in his hands. Then he steps onto the rain butt, tests the lid with his weight, and is up on the lean-to before the barrel stops rocking.

He doesn't stand. He goes flat on the old shingles and slides up toward the wall, keeping his weight on the rafters where the roof is strongest. He stops where the ivy hangs over the top of the wall, and parts it with two fingers until he can see the trough and the cooper's step.

He'll start counting when Hesper's front door opens. Sefa's question is a fair one, and he'll put it to the tiefling himself if he has to. But he wants to see first which way the man runs.

He starts counting when Hesper's front door opens. The alley details you've added (bellows boy, carter, rain butt, lean-to, ivy) fit what we know of the place behind the smithies, so I'll keep them. If something there turns out not to match, I'll say so in one plain line.

The card stands as called: Stealth, DC 15, with his +9. Choosing his moments and keeping to the shade is how a man with his trade does this in broad daylight. That method is already why it's DC 15 and not harder, so it doesn't add advantage on top. What the die decides is whether anyone in the alley or on the street notices a man going up onto a roof. The cart alley is rutted and black with coal grit. On the left the smithies back onto it, open sheds full of heat with a boy working a bellows in one. On the right are yard walls with ivy on them. Up ahead, the cooper's yard is stacked with staves and has a lean-to shed against the wall, roofed in old shingles, low enough to step up onto from a rain butt. A carter is unhitching at the alley's mouth with his back half turned. The bellows boy is watching the coals.

Pell keeps to the ivy side, where the wall's shadow runs along the ruts. He passes the bellows boy between two pumps of the handle, and the boy never lifts his eyes from the coals. At the cooper's wall he steps onto the rain butt's rim and then the lean-to roof, and lies flat along the shingles. Nobody in the alley turns. The roof's ridge meets the cooper's back wall at the height of his chin. Past the corner of the building he can see a slice of the main street: the trough, the corner of the lane, and the cooper's front step at an angle.

The stable lad is still on the edge of the trough. He's finished the bread and is brushing crumbs off his knee, and he watches each cart go by the way a bored boy watches carts. Every so often his eyes drift down Hesper's lane and drift back up. It's no more often than they drift anywhere else.

The tiefling is still in the cooper's doorway. While Pell watches, he straightens, raises his knuckles to the shut door, and holds them there a moment. Then he lowers his hand without knocking and leans on the wall again, arms folded, his jaw set.

Back in the study, the floorboard creaks overhead again, and Hesper comes down. She has a dark cloak over the grey coat. She carries a leather document case under one arm and a drawstring purse in her hand, and she holds the purse the way people hold money they can't spare. "The will, the proving, and a hundred and twenty," she says. "Counted twice." She goes down the hall to the front door and puts her hand on the bar, but she doesn't lift it. It's a little past nine. She waits for Bram and Sefa.

 Pell made it up the alley unseen. The carter, the bellows boy and the two men at the top of the lane never knew he went past. He lies on the cooper's lean-to roof with the street in view, and as far as anyone at the trough or the cooper's step can tell, there's nobody there.

scenes.narration:
Hesper lifts the bar herself. She lays it against the wall, opens the door onto the bright lane and steps out without looking toward the corner. Bram comes out at her right shoulder, his seventeen gold in his purse. Sefa takes the far side, away from the trough, and turns her head down the lane as if she were waiting for the morning cart. Behind them the study is empty. Sefa's seventeen gold lies on the dead man's desk where she left it.

They walk up the lane at Hesper's pace, which is quick and even. The coal cart has finished at the smithy yard. Hammers ring on both sides of them.

Bram watches the corner ahead the way he'd watch a ford before the wagons go in. He looks at the doorways, the shade and the people sitting still. The tiefling in the cooper's doorway sees a man in mail coming and steps down off the step to make room. He ducks his head the way people do when they're used to being looked at. He doesn't watch them pass.

The stable lad does watch them, the way anyone watches a man in mail. Then his eyes go back to the carts. Bram spent ten years in coaching yards, and something about the boy doesn't fit. It's an hour past the bell. At that hour every lad in every inn yard on the Way is mucking out or hauling water, and this one sits on a trough with no horse, no bucket and no fork. Either he's skiving and doesn't care who sees it, or someone is paying him to sit there.

They turn onto the main street. Sefa looks back once at the turn, casually, like a woman checking for traffic. The boy is still on the trough. He hasn't moved and nobody has stood up to follow them. The main street is full of carts, and the doorways are full of people with their own business.

Thole's house stands on the main street, five doors past the cooper's, on the side toward the temple. It's narrow and stone-faced, with a brass-bound door and a small barred grille at head height. A painted board over the lintel reads *G. THOLE, LOANS ON SURETY*. Hesper knocks twice.

The grille opens. A pair of pale eyes looks out at Hesper, then at Bram's shield and mail, then past all three of them at the street. Nobody says anything for a while. Then a bolt slides back, then a second one, and the door opens.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays flat and still, cheek to the warm shingles, breathing slowly through his nose.

*That's not a lookout,* he thinks, watching the tiefling's raised knuckles drop again. *A lookout doesn't knock on the door he's leaning on. That's a man working up the nerve to ask for something, and losing it.* He files it away. A flinch from a tiefling in Beregost these days might mean nothing worse than being tired of being stared at.

The boy is the one he watches more closely. The boy's bored, and boys aren't usually this patient about being bored. The crumbs are gone and he's still sitting there.

Pell doesn't move. He waits for the sound of Hesper's front door, or the sight of Bram's painted shield coming up the lane with two women beside him. When they come, he isn't going to watch them. He'll watch the trough and the step: who looks, who gets up, which way they go, and whether they hurry.

If the boy slides off the trough and heads up the main street, Pell will drop off the far side of the lean-to into the cooper's yard and go out after him, a street behind and on the other side.

*(Passive Insight 14 on the boy while I wait: is he watching the lane on purpose, the way a hired eye does, or is it just idle drifting? And does the tiefling have any business with the cooper, like a tool, a barrel, or a paper in his hand?)*

scenes.narration:
Pell hears the bar come off Hesper's door before he sees anything. It's a dull scrape of wood carried up the lane between hammer strokes. The boy on the trough hears it too. His head doesn't turn, but he stops brushing at his knee, and his hand stays where it is, flat on his thigh, until the door has opened.

Then they come up the lane. Bram's brown-painted shield is at Hesper's right shoulder and Sefa walks on her far side, looking back down the lane as if waiting for a cart. Pell keeps his eyes off them and watches the corner.

The tiefling sees the mail and steps down off the step to make room, with his head ducked. He doesn't look after them, and his eyes go back to the cooper's door before they've passed.

The boy watches them come the way anyone watches a man in mail. Pell has watched a great many people pretend to be bored, and the boy gives himself away afterwards. As the three of them turn onto the main street toward the temple end, a loaded cart comes the other way and blocks his view. The boy puts a hand on the trough's rim and lifts himself up on it, just a few inches, to see past the cart which way they've gone. He holds there until he has seen. Then he sits back down, folds his arms, and lets his eyes drift over the carts again. The boy wasn't curious about them. He was making sure, the way a hired eye does when he knows somebody will ask him later.

He doesn't get up and he doesn't hurry. He leans back on his hands and squints up at the temple tower over the rooftops, the way a man checks the hour when he's being paid by the day.

The tiefling gives Pell a plainer answer. He has a stick in his hand, a length of hazel no longer than a forearm, split down its length. Pell has seen hundreds of them in Lower City yards: a tally, notched across both halves and broken apart, so that the man owed keeps one half and the man who owes keeps the other. He turns it over in his fingers and runs his thumb down the notches. The backs of his hands are pocked with small old burns, the kind iron scale leaves when it flies off the anvil. While Pell watches, the cooper's door opens a crack. A woman in an apron looks out, sees the tiefling and says something short that doesn't carry to the roof. Then she shuts the door. The tiefling puts the tally inside his coat and leans back against the wall. His jaw is set the way it was before.

The bell hasn't rung. A coal cart grinds past the alley mouth below Pell. The boy stays on the trough with his arms folded, and he has settled in to sit there a good while yet.

Nothing else changes at the corner unless Pell moves. He can lie here as long as he likes.

Pell has seen hundreds of them in Lower City yards: a tally, notched across both halves and broken apart, so that the man owed keeps one half and the man who owes keeps the other. He turns it over in his fingers and runs his thumb down the notches. The backs of his hands are pocked with small old burns, the kind iron scale leaves when it flies off the anvil. While Pell watches, the cooper's door opens a crack. A woman in an apron looks out, sees the tiefling and says something short that doesn't carry to the roof. Then she shuts the door. The tiefling puts the tally inside his coat and leans back against the wall. His jaw is set the way it was before.

The bell hasn't rung. A coal cart grinds past the alley mouth below Pell. The boy stays on the trough with his arms folded, and he has settled in to sit there a good while yet.

Nothing else changes at the corner unless Pell moves. He can lie here as long as he likes.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Then let's keep to the writing,” I say evenly. “May we see the rest of that entry, beneath your thumb?”

I stay beside Hesper, hands clear of my sword.

“You're right that a missing ticket leaves a claim unsettled. But how does three hundred gold settle it where a hundred and twenty won't? Would you give her a written release against any later bearer?”

I pause. “And is there a lawful way to cancel the missing ticket before sundown—a declaration before the temple court, or a surety? We'd rather pay for that than buy the same coffer twice.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa hasn't moved from her place behind Hesper's shoulder. She keeps her expression mild, the way you might at a sickbed, and lets her eyes rest on Thole's face while he speaks.

Then, quietly, she says: "You wrote that clause yourself, or you copied it. Either way, it doesn't say two tickets. It says the bearer of *my* ticket, *or* my lawful heir producing it." She gestures once at the document case. "The heir is here, with the proving. Once she redeems, the pledge is ended. A man who came in tomorrow waving a ticket would be waving a dead leaf. The coffer would already be with its owner. You'd carry no debt to him, and the court would say so."

She glances at the heavy dark-green door behind him, then back to his face, and says nothing more.

presses.text:
Sefa lets the silence settle a moment, as she would over a candle flame.

"You're owed a lawful answer, Master Thole, not a guess about whose hand might reach for that ticket." Her voice is warm, unhurried. "Say the heir pays the hundred and twenty now, today, and the entry is closed in your own ledger. What is the stranger's grievance then, and against whom? The pledge is dead because it was redeemed. No writing you hold says a ticket redeems itself after redemption."

She nods at the closed ledger. "If a man came in with the ticket tomorrow—or in a tenday, or a month—he might ask you for the coffer. You would tell him it has gone home to its owner, by the very line he is quoting you, and then his quarrel would be with the Vallow estate, not with Gaspar Thole. But only if the estate has already redeemed. It cannot have both ways."

She looks up at him. "You're asking the widow to pay you extra to protect you from a man who isn't at the counter. The law has a simpler word for that. It's the hundred and twenty in front of you."

Sefa makes her argument quietly. Under *or* there are two roads, she says, and they don't meet. The heir's road ends the pledge, and a pledge that has ended can't be redeemed a second time by anybody. She doesn't press harder. She lets him see that she thinks he already knows it.

Bring it before sundown and I'll take your hundred and twenty, mistress, on this counter, and give you the coffer and my receipt. No three hundred." He wipes his palms again, though only slightly this time. "Without it, the terms stand as written, and at sundown so does Master Ashby's offer."

Hesper hasn't moved. Her purse and her document case still lie on the counter between them. When she answers, she speaks to Thole, but her eyes go to Bram and Sefa.

Thole waits behind his brass rail and doesn't open the ledger.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets the tiefling go from his mind. *A smith's hand owed money by the cooper's wife, and too proud or too frightened to knock. Not ours.* He keeps it in mind anyway, in case it turns out to matter.

The boy is the job. *Paid by the day, reports later. So someone's waiting for him to come and tell them where the widow went.* That's who Pell wants: whoever pays the boy, not the boy himself.

He stays flat and lets the morning pass, easing his weight now and then so the shingles don't creak. He doesn't go down to hurry things along. Every so often he looks to see where the boy's eyes go, whether toward Hesper's lane, toward the temple tower, or up the main street toward Thole's end. If someone stops at the trough to talk to the boy, Pell wants a good look at them: their face, their clothes, and which way they leave.

When the boy finally slides off the trough, Pell counts five breaths. Then he drops down the far side of the lean-to into the cooper's yard, out through the alley, and onto the main street two doors below. He picks the boy up from across the street and well back, with carts and people between them. He keeps his hood down, because hoods get noticed in daylight. He matches the boy's pace and never closes the distance. If the boy stops, Pell stops at a stall and looks at something. If the boy turns into a house or a yard, Pell doesn't follow him in. He notes the door and finds a spot across the way where he can watch who comes out.

If it comes close to the noon bell before the boy moves, Pell stays with the boy anyway. Bram and Sefa know where to look for him, and this is the one chance to see where the boy goes.

*(Stealth +9 to tail him in daylight on the main street, if you need a roll.)*

cards.title: Stealth: sitting still on the chandler's bench across the street while the man in grey looks out through the arch

presses.text:
Pell doesn't look away, and he doesn't freeze. A man who suddenly finds his boots interesting is a man with something to hide. He keeps his eyes where a bored man's eyes would be: half on the chandler's door, half on the street. He scratches the side of his jaw, leans back against the awning post, and lets a cart creak past between him and the arch without seeming to notice he's grateful for it.

*Three of them. A man with a shield. Gone toward the temple end, and toward Thole's.* He runs the boy's hands back in his head. *Two fingers: two women. And that last thing at the hip, small and quick. Asked what the third one carried, maybe. Or asked about me, and the lad never saw me go.*

He turns his head lazily toward the chandler's window, as if checking whether the man inside has finished with whoever's keeping him. He looks at the grey cloak only through the reflection in the bubbled glass.
presses.reply:
Got it. Pell's paragraph goes into the turn as written. He keeps a bored man's eyes, half on the chandler's door and half on the street. He scratches his jaw, leans back on the awning post, and lets the cart creak past between him and the arch. Then he turns lazily toward the chandler's window and watches the grey cloak only in the bubbled glass. The awning post and the window fit a chandler's front on the main street, so I'll keep them.

His reading of the boy's hands is Pell's own guess, and it stays his. Whether two fingers meant two women, and what that last quick touch at the hip asked, isn't confirmed by me. The man in grey's behaviour from here will show whether Pell read it right.

The card stands as called: Stealth, DC 15, with his +9. Not meeting the man's eyes, using the cart and watching through the reflection is exactly the careful, natural cover this check was called for. That is why it's DC 15 and not harder, so it doesn't add advantage on top. Roll when you're ready. Then I'll narrate whether the man in grey's look slides past a bored fellow on a bench, or stops on him.

screens.Pell Dunmore:
You stay flat on the shingles while the morning gets hot.

The sun comes over the cooper's roof. The shingles warm under your chest and smell of old tar. Every few minutes you move your weight from one rafter to the next, slowly, and the roof keeps quiet. Hammers ring from the smithies. Carts go down the main street toward the Way and others come back up it. Twice a dog noses along the alley below you and moves on.

A little after ten the cooper's door opens again, and this time it's the cooper: a broad bald man in a leather apron. He and the tiefling stand close together on the step. Their voices are too low to carry, but you can read the hands well enough. The cooper spreads his palms, the tiefling holds out his half of the hazel tally, and the cooper goes back inside. He comes out with the other half and a small cloth bag. They fit the two halves together and the notches match. The cooper counts coins into the tiefling's palm. It takes him a while, and he counts some of them twice. The tiefling closes his hand, says something short, and walks off down the main street toward the Way. His jaw is still set, but he walks quickly now. The cooper looks at the empty step for a moment, then goes in and shuts the door.

The boy watched all of it with mild interest, the way he watches carts, and then forgot it.

He doesn't forget the lane. For two hours he does nothing a stable lad would do. He doesn't water a horse, fetch a bucket or run an errand. A woman with a basket goes down Hesper's lane and his eyes follow her until she knocks at a door three houses short of the Vallows'. After that they let her go. Once he looks up the main street toward Thole's end, and he looks for longer than idle curiosity would. Twice more he checks the temple tower. Nobody stops at the trough to talk to him. A girl selling cress offers him a bunch and he waves her off.

The sun is almost overhead when he moves. He looks at the tower one last time, slides off the trough, and wipes his hands down his breeches. Then he walks north up the main street, away from the temple and from Thole's, at an easy pace, like a lad going back to work.

You count five breaths. You go down off the far side of the lean-to into the cooper's yard among the stacked staves, out through the alley, and onto the main street two doors below the trough. When you get there, the boy is about a hundred feet ahead with two carts and a knot of smiths' wives between you. You cross to the other side and keep your hood down.

Following him isn't hard. The boy never looks back. He stops once, at a baker's shutter, and spends a copper on a bun. You stop at a cutler's board and turn a paring knife over in your hands until the boy moves on. Beregost's main street runs straight and busy, and you are one more man in it.

At the north end of town the houses thin out and the street widens toward the Trade Way. A coaching inn stands there with a deep arched carriageway and a painted sign of a wheat sheaf, its gold faded nearly to red. The boy goes under the arch without slowing down, like a lad who has walked under it a thousand times. Inside the arch is a cobbled yard with stable doors along one side and a row of horses' heads looking out over them.

You don't follow him in. Across the street a chandler has put a bench out under his awning. You sit on the end of it and settle there like a man waiting for someone inside the shop. Through the arch you can see a slice of the yard about sixty feet away: a mounting block, a water butt, and a side door into the inn.

The boy goes to the water butt and waits there. He waits the way he waited at the trough, except that now he keeps looking at the side door.

The noon bell rings out from the Song of the Morning at the far end of town. On the third stroke the side door opens.

The man who comes out is about forty and dressed for travel, but well. He wears a grey riding cloak thrown back from his shoulders and good boots, and his beard is cut close. He doesn't hurry. He stops in front of the boy and says something, and he smiles as he says it. The boy talks. You can't hear a word at this distance, so you watch the boy's hands. Three fingers go up. Then the boy points back down the street, south, toward the end where Hesper lives. Then two fingers. He slaps his left forearm flat and holds it out from his body, the way a man carries a shield. Then he points south again, and his finger tilts a little toward the temple end.

The man in grey listens without interrupting. When the boy is done, he takes a coin from his purse and puts it in the boy's palm. It's silver; it catches the sun. Then he asks one more question, short. The boy shrugs and draws something vague in the air beside his own hip, small and quick.

The man in grey turns his head and looks out through the arch at the street, slowly, the way a man reads a room he's just walked into.

<<<
Pell Dunmore: Pell lets the tiefling go from his mind. *A smith's hand owed money by the cooper's wife, and too proud or too frightened to knock. Not ours.* He keeps it in mind anyway, in case it turns out to matter.

The boy is the job. *Paid by the day, reports later. So someone's waiting for him to come and tell them where the widow went.* That's who Pell wants: whoever pays the boy, not the boy himself.

He stays flat and lets the morning pass, easing his weight now and then so the shingles don't creak. He doesn't go down to hurry things along. Every so often he looks to see where the boy's eyes go, whether toward Hesper's lane, toward the temple tower, or up the main street toward Thole's end. If someone stops at the trough to talk to the boy, Pell wants a good look at them: their face, their clothes, and which way they leave.

When the boy finally slides off the trough, Pell counts five breaths. He matches the boy's pace and never closes the distance. If the boy stops, Pell stops at a stall and looks at something. If the boy turns into a house or a yard, Pell doesn't follow him in. He notes the door and finds a spot across the way where he can watch who comes out.

If it comes close to the noon bell before the boy moves, Pell stays with the boy anyway. Bram and Sefa know where to look for him, and this is the one chance to see where the boy goes.

*(Stealth +9 to tail him in daylight on the main street, if you need a roll.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Mine can,” I tell Hesper. “I'll ask for a ruling on the clause as written, without naming you. If they require your name, I'll stop and come back to you.”

I turn to Thole. “Put that offer in writing, please: a ruling under the temple seal that the heir's redemption ends the ticket, delivered before sundown, and you'll release the coffer for one hundred and twenty. Copy the exact clause beneath it. Sign it.”

My voice stays matter-of-fact. “That way we bring back what you need, rather than spend the afternoon misunderstanding each other.”

To Hesper, I add, “Keep your money and papers with you for now. We should meet Pell outside before going to the Song.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets out a slow breath, the kind a healer gives when the fever has broken and the patient still isn't safe.

"That's fairer than three hundred," she says quietly to Thole. "You want the temple's voice, not ours. If the court says it, no one can call you faithless." She turns a little so Hesper can see her face. "It doesn't have to be your name. Bram carries your authority. A writing from the court can be asked in your behalf, and the seal goes on the paper—not on you. It's a question of the pledge, not a complaint against you. Your name only stays the applicant's."

scenes.narration:
Hesper listens to Bram without looking away from him. When he says he'll stop and come back to her if the court asks for her name, she nods once.

"Agreed." She turns to Thole. "Write *the heir*. Not my name."

Sefa makes her case to Thole first and then to Hesper, in the same low voice. Thole hears it with his hands folded on the closed ledger. Hesper waits until Sefa has finished.

"The applicant is whoever stands at the clerk's table," she says. "Let that be Master Halloway."

When Sefa turns back to the counter and says *while we're still in the room*, Thole tips his head to her. "On this counter, with you standing where you stand now. I said it, and I'll write it."

He does what Bram asked. He takes a clean sheet from under the counter, uncaps his ink, and then opens the ledger again. This time he turns it toward himself. He copies the clause out of it with his left hand spread flat across the lower half of the page, the way a man shields a hand of cards. He writes slowly, in the same careful hand as the notice, and when he finishes he turns the sheet round on the brass rail so Bram can read it:

*I, Gaspar Thole, lender on surety of Beregost, undertake as follows. If before sundown of this day there is brought to this counter a writing of the court of contracts of the Song of the Morning, under the seal of that court, declaring that the redemption of the coffer by the lawful heir of Master A. Vallow ends the ticket, I will accept one hundred and twenty gold pieces and deliver the said coffer at once, in the presence of the bearer. The clause, as written in my book: "redeemable until sundown of the term by the bearer of my ticket, or my lawful heir producing it." G. Thole, in his own hand.*

Then he writes it out again, word for word, on a second sheet. He sands both. One goes into the ledger between the pages, and he closes the ledger on it. He passes the other across the rail to Bram.

"That one's for the court and for this counter," he says. "I'd sooner it didn't go round the street." His eyes go to the bolted door and come back. "The court of contracts sits in the chapter house behind the temple. Its door is to the left of the great steps. Ask for the warden of contracts. He hears petitions himself."

Hesper keeps her eyes on the paper in Bram's hand while Thole talks about the steps.

When Bram tells her to keep the money and the papers, she lifts the drawstring purse off the counter and puts it inside her cloak. She takes the document case back under her arm.

"I'll go home," she says. "If the court asks for my hand, that's where you'll find me."

Thole stays behind his rail and makes no move toward the street door until someone asks him to. Through the grille a cart goes by outside, and somewhere down the street a smith's hammer starts up again. It isn't ten yet. There are hours left before noon, when you're due to meet Pell at Thole's step or the cooper's corner, and longer still before sundown.

*(Out of game: Hesper and Thole are mine to play, so their answers differ from what Sefa's paragraph had them say. In this scene it's still a little before ten; the noon bell happened only in Pell's thread.)*

 *(Out of game, one line each:)*

1) Bram's request for a ruling isn't made yet. He has to stand before the warden of contracts at the Song first, and the court's answer gets decided when he does.

2) Thole putting his offer in writing needed no roll. He had already made that offer aloud and was glad to have the court carry it, so he wrote and signed it, as the story shows.

3) Keeping the money with Hesper happened: she put the purse inside her cloak and took her case back. Meeting Pell is a plan, and it gets played when Bram and Sefa leave Thole's.

4) Sefa's words needed no new roll. She was holding Thole to terms her earlier Persuasion had already won, and he agreed, then wrote "in the presence of the bearer" into the paper.

messages.text:
Pell gives it a slow count of thirty after the side door shuts. Then he stands, stretches like a man tired of waiting, and steps into the chandler's shop out of the sun.

He picks out the cheapest tallow dip on the board and puts two coppers down for it. He keeps his voice easy, one tradesman's gossip to another.

"Your neighbour's got quality in." He tips his head toward the arch. "Grey cloak, good boots, beard cut like a Waterdhavian's. Looks like a man who buys beeswax, not this." He turns the dip in his fingers. "Been here long? He and that big lad in the upstairs window?"

He doesn't name Ashby. If the chandler offers a name, Pell lets it go by like it means nothing to him. Whatever he gets, he thanks the man, pockets the candle, and goes.

He doesn't go back down the main street the way he came. He takes the first side lane that runs south, behind the houses, then cuts back onto the main street halfway down. Twice he stops in a doorway, as if to shake a stone from his boot, and watches the way he came for anyone who stops when he stops.

Then he heads for Thole's step, and the cooper's corner after that if the others aren't there. He's late by the bell, and he said the rest would come looking.

When he finds Bram and Sefa, he keeps it short and quiet:

"Your watcher's a stable lad at the Red Sheaf, north end. Paid in silver by a man in a grey riding cloak, about forty, travelling money. He's got a sellsword upstairs with his boots on the sill. The lad told him all three of you went out, the shield, and that you turned toward the temple end. Then the grey man asked him something, and the lad made a little sign at his hip." He shows it: small and quick. "I'd lay odds that's Ashby. How did Thole take the money?"

*(Out of game: I'll keep the Inspiration. If the chandler wants a roll to loosen up, Pell offers to buy something better than tallow.)*

scenes.narration:
Pell sits out a slow count of thirty after the side door closes. Then he gets up, rolls the stiffness out of his shoulders like a man who has given up on his wife ever finishing, and steps under the awning into the chandler's shop.

Inside it's dim and smells of tallow and warm wax. Candles hang by their wicks in bunches from the beams. A lean man in his fifties stands behind a board scarred with knife cuts. His cuffs are crusted white with drips and he has a pencil behind one ear. He watches Pell take the cheapest dip off the board and put two coppers down beside it. He sweeps them into his palm without looking at them.

At the quip about beeswax he gives a short laugh through his nose.

"Beeswax? Not him, friend. Lamp oil." He jerks his thumb toward the arch across the street. "Two flasks yesterday, the good clear stuff, and a new tinderbox. Paid on the nail. He's been at the Sheaf near a tenday. Iron buyer, they say. The forges down the street like him, because he pays ahead." He takes the pencil from behind his ear and taps a slate hanging on a nail by the door. Among the chalked sums someone has written in a neat, sloping hand: *Ashby & Corve. 2 fl. oil. Paid.* "Wrote that himself, when I said I like a name for my book. Like he was a firm." He puts the pencil back. "The big one upstairs came in with him. So did another one, a thin fellow who rides out early and comes back after dark. The big one sits in that window all day like a cat on a wall. Never buys so much as a wick."

Pell lets the name go past as though it were just another sum on the slate. He thanks the man, puts the dip in his coat and goes out into the glare.

He doesn't take the main street. A little way south he finds a side lane between a saddler's and a bakehouse. It runs behind the houses past middens, washing lines and a goat tied to a cart wheel, and he follows it. At the first bend he stops in a gateway, bends to his boot and shakes out a stone that isn't there. The lane behind him is empty except for the goat.

Halfway down the town he cuts back through a passage onto the main street. He stops in a cobbler's doorway and fusses with his boot again, and watches the street.

The sunburnt man is out on the main street, coming south. He has his sleeves rolled down now and a plain brown jerkin on, and the sword belt is buckled at his hip instead of hanging on a shutter-hook. He walks down the middle of the street at an easy, rolling pace, like a man with somewhere to be and plenty of time to get there. He doesn't look into side lanes or doorways. He looks ahead, toward the temple end. He passes the cobbler's doorway about thirty feet off and never turns his head. He isn't following anyone. He's going somewhere.

Pell lets him get well ahead before he steps out. He doesn't have to follow, because they're going the same way.

By the time the Song of the Morning's tower looms over the rooftops, it's getting on for one o'clock. Pell can see Thole's narrow stone front with its brass-bound door and painted board. The grille is shut. Across the street and three doors up there's an alehouse with a serving hatch on the street and a bench under it. The sunburnt man stops at the hatch and buys a cup. He sits down on the end of the bench, stretches his legs out and drinks slowly. From where he sits he can see Thole's door, the street in both directions, and past the last roofs the foot of the temple's great steps.

He looks like a man settling in for the afternoon. Thole's step is about a hundred feet ahead of Pell, in plain view of the bench.

*(Out of game: Bram and Sefa's thread is still a little before ten. Whether they're on Thole's step or at the cooper's corner at one o'clock depends on their next rounds, so the threads join when theirs catches up. From here, what Pell does with the man on the bench is up to you.)*

 *(Out of game, one line each:)*

1) Pell's count of thirty needed no roll. Nothing was uncertain, and he did it before stepping under the awning, as the turn shows.

2) Buying the dip and chatting needed no roll. Easy gossip with a shopkeeper who's just been paid is routine for Pell, and the chandler had nothing to hide. He gave the name *Ashby & Corve* off his own slate without Pell asking for it.

3) Checking for followers needed no roll. Nobody was following him, so there was nothing to beat. He stopped twice, and the lane and the street were clear. The sunburnt man walked past him on his way somewhere else and never looked his way.

4) Pell got within sight of Thole's step, about 100 feet off, and the turn stopped there. Where Bram and Sefa are at one o'clock is decided by their own rounds, and their thread is still just before ten. Now that a hired sword sits watching that door, whether Pell walks onto the step is his call.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I read the undertaking through, then fold it carefully into my pack.

“Thank you. The door, please, Master Thole.”

Once we're outside, I speak quietly to Hesper and Sefa. “We'll walk you home first. It's barely a detour, and you have the redemption money on you.”

On the walk, I ask Hesper, “The undertaking names Aubrey. May I show it to the warden, provided I neither name you nor present your authority? I don't want to keep the letter of our promise and break its meaning.”

I glance to Sefa. “Then the chapter house, if you're willing. We'll return here by noon for Pell.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa gives Thole a last small nod, the kind that closes a bargain without haste.

"You've kept your side of the counter clean, and we'll keep ours." She lets her hands stay in sight as she steps back from the rail. "If Ashby comes early and asks why his offer isn't the one you took before sundown, tell him the term isn't ended yet."

She turns with the others, but while Bram takes the folded undertaking she glances once, without any obvious insistence, at the closed ledger under Thole's palm. Not at the clause—at the parts he shielded. She doesn't reach for it, only files it away.

Outside, on the step, she keeps her voice down and her eyes on the street. "To the corner, then. If Pell isn't there when the bell goes, one of us should go for Hesper's door and one to the temple steps." A pause. "He may have followed the tiefling. Let's hope he bought one of us something more than a sore foot."

scenes.narration:
Thole hears Sefa out with his hand still flat on the closed ledger.

"Until sundown the term is hers, mistress. I'll tell anyone who asks exactly that." He comes out from behind the rail. Before he touches the bolts he looks out through the grille at the street, the way a man checks the weather. Then he draws both bolts and opens the door onto the noise of the main street. "Before sundown," he says to Bram, and nothing more. The door shuts behind them, and the first bolt slides home before they've left the step.

Sefa had looked once at the ledger as they turned to go. Thole kept his palm across the cover the whole time. Under it the corner of the second copy stuck out between the pages, the one he'd closed in there himself. That was all there was to see.

On the step Hesper settles the document case under her arm and listens to Bram.

"Home, then." She doesn't argue about the detour. She sets off the way she came, at the same quick, even pace, with the purse inside her cloak and one hand over it.

They walk back up the main street toward the cooper's corner. As they come level with the cooper's, the shop door opens and a broad, bald man in a leather apron steps out onto the step. The tiefling in the road-dusty coat is still there. He takes something from inside his coat: half a split hazel stick, notched across. The cooper fits his own half against it, the two halves line up, and he starts counting coins into the tiefling's palm out of a cloth bag. Bram spent ten years on the Way watching drovers get paid off at the end of a run, and he knows what this is. It's a tally, and a man who has waited a good while for his wages is finally being paid them. Sefa sees it too. If Pell followed anyone this morning, it wasn't this man.

The stable lad is still on the trough. He watches the three of them turn down the lane, mildly, the way he watches carts.

Halfway down the lane Bram asks his question. Hesper doesn't slow her pace or turn her head to answer.

"Show it. Aubrey's name was in Thole's book before mine was anywhere." A few steps go by. "The court knows who his heir is. They proved the will in the spring, so my name went into their book once already. Once is enough." She shifts the case under her arm. "My letter is for treating with Thole. Keep it for Thole. If the warden wants to know who you're acting for, tell him you're acting on the undertaking. That's true."

At her own door she takes a key from her cloak, opens the lock and stands on the threshold with the door half open behind her. She puts her inked hand flat on the oak.

"I'll be here until sundown. If the court wants anything from me, send word and I'll come down to the step and sign it. Not past the step." She looks at Bram, then at Sefa. "The chapter house is open from the second bell. Thole was right about the door. It's on the left of the great steps."

Then she goes in, and they hear the bar drop on the inside.

It's about a quarter past ten. The lane rings with hammers, and the noon bell is a long way off.

*(Out of game: I left this out of Pell's thread. From the roof he would have seen Bram, Sefa and Hesper come back down the lane a little after ten, just before the cooper paid the tiefling. He saw it, and it changes nothing he did.)*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't step out of the cobbler's doorway. From there he sweeps the street ahead slowly: the painted shield, a grey coat beside it, Sefa. He checks Thole's step, the alehouse hatch, and the mouth of every lane between here and the temple.

*Sitting on Thole's door with the steps in view. So Ashby knows where the widow went, and now he wants to know whether she comes out with anything.* Then he thinks of the slate. *Lamp oil, the good clear stuff, and a new tinderbox. A man buying iron doesn't need either.* He doesn't like what that adds up to, with a coffer sitting in a moneylender's back room.

He won't walk the last hundred feet past that bench. If the others aren't in sight, he backs out the way he came, through the passage and down the lane behind the houses. Then he circles south and east to come at the cooper's corner from the cart alley behind the smithies, out of the sunburnt man's view. If they've given up on Thole's step, that's where they'll be, or on their way back to Hesper's.

If he does spot them on the street and they're heading toward Thole's or the bench, he doesn't wave or call. He drifts into their path from a side lane, falls in beside Bram for three steps, and says low, without looking at him: "Don't look at the alehouse bench. Big sunburnt man with a cup. He's Ashby's, and he's watching that door. Keep walking. Cooper's yard, back way."

*(Passive Perception 14 for the others on the street. Does Thole's shop have a back way or a yard I can see from a side lane on the way round? I'd note it for later without going near it.)*

scenes.narration:
Pell stays in the cobbler's doorway with one boot up on the step and looks down the street, one stretch at a time.

The sunburnt man is on the alehouse bench with his cup, his legs stretched out into the street. A carter has to swing wide of his boots and swears at him, and the man doesn't pull them in. Across the way Thole's brass-bound door is shut and the grille is closed. While Pell watches, the grille slides open a finger's width. Pale eyes look out at the street, settle on the bench for a long moment, then the grille closes again. The man on the bench doesn't seem to notice, or he doesn't care whether he's seen.

The rest of the street is ordinary early afternoon. A smith's wife has a basket of loaves on her hip. Two Amnian-looking drovers argue over a halter. A boy is chasing a hen out of a doorway. Between the cobbler's and the temple Pell picks out the mouth of every side lane: a passage by a farrier's, a gap with washing strung across it, a covered way under a bakehouse. Nobody is loitering in any of them. On the stretch of street he can see, there's no brown-painted shield, no grey coat and no Sefa.

So he backs out the way he came, back through the passage onto the lane behind the houses, past the goat on its cart wheel. From there he turns east and south behind the houses on the smithies' side. The back lanes are midden-walls, kitchen doors, and a woman scrubbing a pot on her step who doesn't look up. After a few minutes the lane narrows between two yard walls and comes out into the cart alley behind the smithies, which is rutted and black with coal grit, the same as it was this morning. The bellows boy is still at his handle.

The cooper's yard has a footway behind it. Its staves are stacked and the lean-to roof where Pell lay is empty in the sun. The footway runs on toward the temple end along the backs of the main-street houses, too narrow for a cart. Pell doesn't go down it. He stops at its mouth as if to retie a lace and counts the back walls by their chimneys.

The fifth wall past the cooper's stands higher than its neighbours, close to ten feet of grey stone with fresh limewash. Broken crockery is set in mortar along the top, the way careful men in the Lower City top their walls. In it there's a single narrow door, iron-studded, flush with the stone, with no handle on this side that he can see. Above it, on the upper floor, is one shuttered window. Low down near the foot of the wall, just above the dirt of the footway, is a small square vent, barred with three iron rods, black inside. Nothing about it says what room it breathes for. All the other houses along that row have kitchen doors and slop-drains, and this one has neither.

Pell finishes with the lace and walks the last few yards up the alley to the cooper's yard gate. Past the corner of the cooper's house he can see the main street. The trough at the top of Hesper's lane stands empty. Nobody's sitting on its rim now, and there's only a wet ring on the stone where someone set a bucket down. Down the lane Hesper's door is shut and her shutters are closed. It's a little past a quarter after one.

*(Out of game: Bram and Sefa weren't on the stretch of street Pell could see at that moment. Where they are at one o'clock, and whether they're at the cooper's corner, depends on their own thread, which is still at about a quarter past ten. No roll was needed: Pell was already unseen, and he backed away without anyone looking his way.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I wait until the bar settles, then turn toward the main street with Sefa.

“The tiefling was waiting for wages. Saw his tally match the cooper's. The boy's still idle at the trough, though. We'll tell Pell when we meet him.”

I keep my voice low as we walk. “At the court, I'll show Thole's undertaking and ask whether they can give the ruling it requires. No authority letter, no petition in Hesper's name.”

I head for the chapter house door to the left of the temple steps. Once inside, I approach whoever receives petitioners.

“Bram Halloway. I'd like to speak with the warden of contracts about a pledge that falls due at sundown. The lender has put the question in writing.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa watches the door until the bar drops, then turns to Bram.

"Then the chapter house now. If its door isn't open yet, we sit on the great steps and watch the morning go—there are worse places to think." She starts back toward the main street, keeping close to the lane's far side. "When we're inside, let me put the question as a point of law before you hand over anything with your name on it. A dead notary's pledge, a lender's written undertaking, and the clause itself. The warden can rule on that, if he's the kind who likes a clean line. And we want his seal, not his pity."

She glances at the temple roof ahead, then at Bram's pack. "Thole swore no word of Hesper and no word of the widow. But he knows the heir is established. If the warden asks whose interest is served, tell him it's the repayment of a debt and the return of property—both of which the court has an interest in seeing done before sundown."

scenes.narration:
Hesper's bar drops into its brackets with a dull knock. Bram turns back up the lane, and Sefa falls in beside him on the far side, close to the wall.

She hears him out about the tiefling and the boy, then nods once at the trough as they pass it. The boy is still sitting there. His eyes follow the mail up to the corner and let it go, the way they did before.

On the main street Sefa keeps her voice under the noise of the carts and lays out what she'd like to do: put the question as a point of law, and ask for the seal rather than the warden's sympathy. Then she adds what to say if anyone asks whose interest is served: a debt repaid, property returned, both before sundown.

The Song of the Morning stands at the south end of town, where the main street widens into a square paved in pale stone. The temple is rose-coloured granite, with a tower and a great flight of steps going up to doors painted gold. A novice with a broom is working down the steps one at a time, and a pair of drovers have stopped at the bottom to drink from the fountain. As Bram and Sefa cross the square the bell starts up in the tower: two strokes, then quiet. It's the second bell.

The door Thole told them about is set into the chapter house wall, left of the great steps. It's a plain oak door with a sun-disc carved over the lintel, and as they reach it a lay brother opens it from inside and props it with a wedge. Beyond is a whitewashed antechamber with benches along two walls and a high window. A young brother in a saffron tabard sits at a table with an open book, a sand-box and a rack of pens. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stands at the cooper's gate a moment longer and looks at the empty trough and the wet ring on the stone.

*Nobody here. They went to Thole's, and the grille's shut. So either he turned them away and they went home, or they're out looking for me, which is what I told them to do.* He hopes it's the first. Three people searching Beregost for a man nobody's supposed to notice would undo his whole morning.

He doesn't take the lane. He goes back down the cart alley, past the bellows boy, to the door under the pear tree. It's still nearly shut, the way he left it. He listens at the gap first for voices in the yard or the study. Then he lifts the door on its hinges again so it won't scrape, slips through, and draws it closed and slides the bolt home behind him.

At the study's back window he raps twice on the frame, softly, so whoever is inside knows it's him and not the lane.

If they're inside, he comes in and keeps it quiet:

"Sorry I'm late. I was following the lad." He tells it plainly. "The watcher's a stable boy at the Red Sheaf, north end. A man in a grey riding cloak pays him in silver at the noon bell. The chandler across the way has him chalked on his slate as *Ashby & Corve*. He's an iron buyer by his own account, been there near a tenday. He bought two flasks of good lamp oil and a new tinderbox yesterday." He lets that sit. "He has two men with him. A thin one rides out early and comes back after dark. The big sunburnt one is on the alehouse bench across from Thole's right now with a cup, watching the door and the temple steps. Thole's seen him through the grille."

He looks at Bram, then Hesper. "So tell me about Thole."

If the house is empty, he doesn't wait in it. He writes a single line on a scrap from the desk, *Back by the yard. Waiting at the cooper's gate. P.*, and leaves it under the purse's dent on the desk. Then he goes out the way he came and keeps watch on the trough from the yard gate.

*(Out of game: Thole's back wall is the fifth chimney past the cooper's. It's high, limewashed and topped with crockery, with a flush iron-studded door and a barred vent near the ground. I'm noting it, not going near it.)*

scenes.narration:
Pell goes back down the cart alley the way he came. The bellows boy is still working his handle and doesn't look up. The door under the pear tree stands as he left it, a finger's width open. He listens at the gap. The yard is quiet except for a wasp working at the windfalls in the grass. No voices come from the house.

He lifts the door on its hinges, slips through, and lets it settle closed without a scrape. The bolt is easier going home than it was coming back, now that the rust has been worked. He crosses the yard past the rain barrel and raps twice, softly, on the frame of the study's back window.

For a moment nothing happens. Then a floorboard creaks somewhere inside. The study door opens a crack, and then all the way. Hesper comes in still wearing her grey coat, though the cloak is off. She holds the iron poker from the cold hearth low against her skirt. When she sees who's at the glass she puts it back where it came from, unhurried, and unlatches the window.

"Master Dunmore." Her eyes take in the coal grit on his knees and the tar on his coat front. "They aren't here."

She rests her inked hand flat on the sill.

"They brought me home at a quarter past ten. Thole won't take my hundred and twenty without a ticket, unless the temple's court of contracts gives him a writing under its seal saying the heir's redemption ends the ticket. If they bring that before sundown, he takes the money and hands over the coffer on his counter. He put it in writing. Master Halloway carries it." Behind her, two piles of seventeen gold lie on the desk where they were left this morning. "They went from my door to the chapter house. I haven't seen either of them since."

She glances once past him at the yard door, at the bolt he has just slid home, and then back to his face.

"The trough has been empty since noon. I looked from upstairs." She doesn't ask whether that was his doing. She asks the other thing. "Did you find out who sends him?"

*(Out of game: Bram and Sefa aren't here, so neither of the plans you set fits exactly. Hesper is home alone, and what you tell her is up to you.)*

 *(Out of game, one line each:)*

1) This happened and needed no roll. Pell went back down the alley, bolted the yard door behind him and rapped twice on the study window, and Hesper came to it.

2) Pell's report was meant for when Bram and Sefa were inside. They aren't there, and Hesper ended the turn by asking Pell who sends the watcher, so what he tells her and how much is your answer to give.

3) That line belonged to the same "if they're inside" plan, so Pell didn't say it. Hesper told him Thole's terms herself anyway: the court's sealed writing, the hundred and twenty, and the undertaking Bram carries.

4) The house isn't empty because Hesper is home, so the branch with the note and the wait at the cooper's gate didn't happen. Pell is still free to leave a note or go back to the gate after he answers her.

*(Correction: I wrote that two piles of seventeen lie on the desk. Bram took his share this morning, so only one pile is there, Sefa's seventeen gold.)*

Pell Dunmore: Pell stands at the cooper's gate a moment longer and looks at the empty trough and the wet ring on the stone.

*Nobody here. They went to Thole's, and the grille's shut. So either he turned them away and they went home, or they're out looking for me, which is what I told them to do.* He hopes it's the first. Three people searching Beregost for a man nobody's supposed to notice would undo his whole morning.

He doesn't take the lane. He goes back down the cart alley, past the bellows boy, to the door under the pear tree. It's still nearly shut, the way he left it. He listens at the gap first for voices in the yard or the study. Then he lifts the door on its hinges again so it won't scrape, slips through, and draws it closed and slides the bolt home behind him.

At the study's back window he raps twice on the frame, softly, so whoever is inside knows it's him and not the lane.

If they're inside, he comes in and keeps it quiet:

"Sorry I'm late. I was following the lad." He tells it plainly. "The watcher's a stable boy at the Red Sheaf, north end. A man in a grey riding cloak pays him in silver at the noon bell. The chandler across the way has him chalked on his slate as *Ashby & Corve*. He's an iron buyer by his own account, been there near a tenday. He bought two flasks of good lamp oil and a new tinderbox yesterday." He lets that sit. "He has two men with him. A thin one rides out early and comes back after dark. The big sunburnt one is on the alehouse bench across from Thole's right now with a cup, watching the door and the temple steps. Thole's seen him through the grille."

He looks at Bram, then Hesper. "So tell me about Thole."

If the house is empty, he doesn't wait in it. He writes a single line on a scrap from the desk, *Back by the yard. Waiting at the cooper's gate. P.*, and leaves it under the purse's dent on the desk. Then he goes out the way he came and keeps watch on the trough from the yard gate.

*(Out of game: Thole's back wall is the fifth chimney past the cooper's. It's high, limewashed and topped with crockery, with a flush iron-studded door and a barred vent near the ground. I'm noting it, not going near it.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Master Corwen Ashby. Thole says he's offered two hundred and fifty gold, payable at sundown. He hasn't asked Thole about a ticket. That's all we know of his claim.”

I leave the undertaking on the table.

“Thole first asked three hundred to release the coffer without the ticket. Then he agreed to the original hundred and twenty if we brought your ruling. He seemed concerned about the buyer as well as any later bearer.”

I take out two gold pieces, but pause before setting them down.

“I can pay the fee. First, I need to be clear: I'm asking in my own name, on this undertaking. Would the entry name only Aubrey's pledge and me as applicant, without entering his widow as a petitioner?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa sits when she is asked, and sets her folded hands on the table's edge as though the whitewashed room were an extension of the hospice.

"Another man wants it," she says evenly. "By the lender's account, a buyer with more money and no ticket. He's offered more, and by the terms he can't so much as touch the coffer until the term ends at sundown. So he hasn't come to this hearing. If he had, you'd have two people at the table."

She doesn't say the name. She lets it lie with the rest of what the warden already knows.

"A widow has come to a lender to pay what the pledge says. The lender won't take it, not because she's failed the terms, but because the paper he wrote is two ways round at once. He's written us a promise instead: if the court gives a true reading of his own clause, he'll accept the lawful redemption. That's the whole quarrel. It's a matter of what the words mean before sundown." She pauses. "Whatever the coffer holds, and whoever else would like to carry it off, no one at this table is asking you to choose between two people. We're asking you to say what the clause means."
