screens.text:
The session begins.

Beregost is already at work. Hammers ring from the smithies down the lane, a cart rattles past toward the Trade Way, and the last note of Lathander's morning bell fades over the rooftops.

The oak door opens a hand's width, then wider. Hesper Vallow stands in the gap. She is a spare woman in a plain grey coat, ink on two fingers of her right hand. She looks at each of you in turn: you with your painted-over shield, Sefa, and Pell. Then her gaze goes past you, up the lane toward the main street, and stays there a moment too long.

"All three of you. Good." Behind her the hall is dim. Every shutter on the ground floor is closed against the sun. "By nightfall, as I said. Not an hour later." She steps back from the threshold and holds the door, but she doesn't explain yet. She is waiting to see who comes in first, or whether anyone has something to ask her out here on the step.

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10
Skills: Athletics +6; Perception +4; Survival +4; Intimidation +3; Tools: land vehicles +3
Saves: Strength saving throw +6 (proficient); Constitution saving throw +5 (proficient); Dexterity saving throw +1; Intelligence saving throw +0; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +0
Attacks: Longsword +6 to hit, 1d8+3 slashing (1d10+3 two-handed); Javelin +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 30/120; Extra Attack: two attacks with the Attack action
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Extra Attack: attacks twice when taking the Attack action; Fighting style, Protection: with a shield, a reaction imposes disadvantage on an attack against a creature within 5 feet of him; Second Wind: a bonus action, regains 1d10+5 hit points; once per short rest; Action Surge: one additional action on his turn; once per short rest; Improved Critical (Champion): a weapon attack crits on 19 or 20; Healer's kit: stabilises a dying creature without a check (ten uses)
Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Second wind 1/1; Action surge 1/1
Money: 23 gp; 14 sp; 30 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: on the step outside Hesper Vallow's oak door, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa comes in right behind you, unhurried, and gives Hesper a small nod. "Nightfall, then," she says quietly. "We'll hear it inside, I think. Better than on the step."

Pell's eyes follow yours up the lane a moment after you look. He takes in the main street and the doorways before he looks back at Hesper and keeps his voice low. "You looked up that lane like you were expecting someone. Worth knowing who, before we hear the rest." He pauses on the threshold and nods at the closed shutters. "And if it's the sort of someone who watches doors, I'd rather we talk in a room without windows to the street."

It's an ordinary Beregost morning. A coal cart is backing into the smithy yard at the bottom of the lane. At the top, where the lane meets the main street, a horse trough stands by the corner. A stable lad sits on its edge with straw on his sleeves, picking at a heel of bread and watching the carts. Across from him, in the shade of the cooper's doorway, a tiefling in a road-dusty coat stands by the wall.

You go in first, sword sheathed, and step to the left of the doorway. Sefa comes right behind you. Pell comes last, out of the sun, and stops where he can still see a hand's width of the lane through the gap.

The hall smells of beeswax and cold ashes. Hesper shuts the door, drops the bar, and stands a moment with her palm flat on the oak.

"Someone has stood at the top of the lane three mornings running," she says. "Young, I think. I see him from the upstairs window, and never well. I don't know who he is. I don't know who sends him." She looks at Pell. "You're right about the street. Come through."

She takes you down the hall, past a front room where the furniture sits under dust sheets, to a study at the back. Its one window looks onto a walled yard with a rain barrel and a pear tree. Shelves of bound ledgers cover two walls. A notary's desk sits under the window, tidy and unused, with a rack of seal-stamps and a dish of red wax that has gone dull with dust. Hesper doesn't sit. She stands behind the desk, her inked hand resting on its edge.

"My husband was Aubrey Vallow, notary of this town for twenty years. He died this winter. He fell on the steps of the Song of the Morning." She says it like an entry in a register. "Eight months ago he pledged an iron coffer to a moneylender on the main street, Gaspar Thole. I didn't know until last week, when Thole sent me a courtesy notice as the widow. The term of the pledge ends at sundown today. After that, Thole may sell it, and he has a buyer. A Master Corwen Ashby. I don't know him."

"I have been to Thole twice. The first time he was polite and told me nothing. The second time he didn't open the door."

From a drawer she takes a leather purse and sets it on the desk. It's heavy, and it stays where she put it.

"The terms. I want the coffer brought here, to this room, before sundown. Fifty gold now, a hundred more on delivery. How you get it from Thole is your affair, provided nothing is done that puts my name before the temple court. And one condition, which isn't negotiable." She raises her eyes to each of you in turn. "It comes to me shut. Not opened, not tried, not looked into. Aubrey asked me to keep it shut, and I mean to."

She waits with her hand beside the purse and doesn't push it toward any of you.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Aubrey Vallow's coffer
+ Quest: Aubrey Vallow's coffer

Where you are: Hesper's back study · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa folds her hands in front of her and makes no move toward the purse. "We'll take it on. But before that purse changes hands, tell us three things plainly," she says, her voice low and even. "Do you have Aubrey's note of pledge—the number of the debt, the surety written? If we walk into Thole's shop with nothing but a widow's word, he can name any sum and shut the door again." She glances at the closed window and back to Hesper. "And the coffer itself. You said iron. Is it small enough to carry under one arm, or will we need a cart and two strong backs? Has it any mark we can swear to—a scratch, a lockplate, a letter, a way of proving it is your husband's and not some other man's coffer?" A pause. "And the watcher at the top of the lane. These three mornings—when does he stop? Does he stay after the doors open, or only until someone shows at a window? Thole may not have been as courteous as his notice."

Pell doesn't reach for the purse. He glances back down the hall toward the barred door, then at Hesper. "Your watcher might have company. There's a tiefling in a road coat in the cooper's doorway, across from the trough. He turned away when I looked at him, quicker than a man with nothing to hide. The stable lad didn't turn at all. So either one of them is yours, or there are two of them." He shrugs. "Worth knowing before we walk out of here carrying anything."

He nods at the shelves of ledgers. "Here's the part I care about. A pledge has a price to buy it back. What did Aubrey borrow against it, and what does Thole want by sundown? If you can just pay it, the easiest way to get your coffer is to walk in the front door with the money, and nobody goes near a temple court. And a notary of twenty years doesn't pledge anything without writing it down. Did he keep his copy of the contract? The pledge note, a receipt, a ledger entry with Thole's name on it? If that paper's in this room, it's worth more to us than any lockpick."

He leaves a beat, then asks the last question more quietly. "I won't open it. You have my word, and I keep that one. But I'd like to know what I'm carrying, at least from the outside. How big is it, how heavy, and is there a key? Does Thole have one, or did Aubrey keep it?"

Nobody touches the purse. Hesper looks at it, then at you, as though you had asked the right question first.

"The fifty is yours. It's yours whatever Thole asks." She opens the drawer again and lays a folded sheet beside the purse. It has been opened and closed so often it lies flat along its creases. "His notice. Read it."

It's written in a careful moneylender's hand that takes care over the figures. *To the widow of Master Aubrey Vallow.* One coffer of iron, banded, small enough for one man to carry, its hasp sealed in yellow wax, deposited by the said Master Vallow eight months since, against a loan of one hundred and twenty gold pieces. Redeemable until sundown of this day *by the bearer of the ticket, or the lawful heir producing it.* After that it falls forfeit to the undersigned. A buyer, Master Corwen Ashby, has declared his interest. *G. Thole, in his own hand.*

"A hundred and twenty," Hesper says. "If he'll take it lawfully, I'll pay it, and your hundred still stands. I can't go far past that." She answers your other question in the same even tone. "I'm his widow and his heir. The will was proved before the temple court in the spring, and I hold the copy. I showed it to Thole the first time. He read it twice and said the terms stand as written. He wouldn't tell me whether that meant he'd take my money." A pause. "I have no ticket. There's no copy of the pledge in this house. I've been through his papers. It's the only paper I ever knew him not to keep."

She turns to Sefa. "I never saw the coffer. What you've just read is all I know of it." She tips her chin at the rack of stamps and the dish of dull red wax. "Aubrey sealed in red. Every stamp in that rack is his, and every one takes red."

To Pell: "If there's a key, I haven't found it. The notice doesn't mention one."

Then back to your last question. "I don't know what's in it. Nobody has warned me of anything. That notice is the only word anyone has sent me about it. Aubrey told me once, in this room: if it ever comes to you, keep it shut. He didn't say why, and I didn't ask." She answers that one faster than the others, and her eyes stay on the wax dish while she does.

The watcher next. "He's there when I open the upstairs shutters, before the bell. By the time I sit down to eat at noon, he's gone. It's been the same three days running. I don't know where he goes." She looks at Pell. "From upstairs I can see the corner, the trough, the cooper's step and a hat. I couldn't tell you which of them it is, or whether it's the same one every morning." To Sefa, flatly: "He was courteous the first time. The second time he was in. I saw his lamp."

At Pell's promise she holds his eyes a moment longer than she has held anyone's. "I'll hold you to that."

When he looks at the shelves, she hesitates. Then she takes down two narrow books bound in calf, this year's and last year's, and sets them on the desk. "The day-books. Not the registers. Those are his clients' business, not mine to open."

Pell sits down at the dead man's desk and starts turning pages. He reads a long while, back through the year and into the one before, and at last his finger comes to rest on a page.

Hesper looks where his finger rests. "Sister Maudra Kell keeps the temple archive. Aubrey did the temple's leases and bequests for years. I saw those entries." Her eyes move to the margin and stay there. "That mark I don't know. It isn't one of his."

The bell of the Song of the Morning hasn't rung again. Half an hour has gone by since you came in off the lane, and the purse still sits on the desk where she put it.

Where you are: Aubrey Vallow's study, Hesper's house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa steps to the desk without taking the notice from Hesper's side and bends a little over the open day-book. "Show me exactly where the margin mark lies," she says to Pell. "The widow says it isn't Aubrey's hand. If it's writing of any kind, I may be able to read it."

Her eyes move from the mark to the entries around it, then she looks up at Hesper. "Thole's wording is a leash with two knots. 'The bearer of the ticket' he has never given you, and 'the lawful heir producing it'. Producing the ticket, the will, or the coffer? A temple clerk could argue that for a month. We have until sundown, so we won't argue unless we must." A pause. "His notice says the pledge ended because the ticket is lost. But a notary of twenty years kept a day-book. If Aubrey wrote what was pledged and to whom, and some other hand put a mark beside it, that mark may tell us whether Thole has been here once already to tidy his side of the shelf."

Pell takes Aubrey's pen from its rest. It's dry, so he dips it once in the inkwell and copies the mark onto a scrap of paper: the circle, the upright stroke, the little hook at the foot. His hand is steady. He blows the ink dry and tucks the scrap inside his coat. Then he finally reaches over and takes the purse, weighs it once in his palm, and sets it down nearer the middle of the desk.

"We'll take it." He turns the notice so you can both see one line, and taps it. "*By the bearer of the ticket, or the lawful heir producing it.* That's a moneylender's way of saying the ticket comes first. Aubrey kept every paper he ever touched except this one. So either he hid it, or he gave it to someone. If it's in a stranger's hand by sundown, Thole can hand the coffer over and call it lawful, and your will won't stop him. I'd wager Master Ashby knows where that ticket is, even if we don't."

He looks at you and Sefa. "Here's how I'd cut it. Mistress Vallow goes to Thole with the hundred and twenty and the will, and she doesn't go alone. One of you walks in beside her. He shut his door on a widow. He won't do that to a man in chain mail with a writ in her hand, not in daylight on the main street. If he takes the money, we're done by noon." A pause. "If he won't, I want to know why. And I want to know where Thole keeps things, and whether Ashby has already been in to see it."

He nods toward the front of the house. "Our watcher leaves before noon. I'd like to see where he goes. I'll slip out the back over the yard wall and pick him up from the corner. The tiefling first, since he's the one who flinched." He holds up the folded scrap. "Then the temple. Sister Kell saw Aubrey twice in her archive, and this mark sits beside the second visit. If it's a temple sign, she'll know it. If it isn't, her face will tell me."

To Hesper, more quietly: "Is the yard gate barred, and does it come out on another lane? I'd rather nobody sees four of us leave by your front door."

You step up beside the desk. The day-book lies open where Pell left it, and the entry is easy to read: *Song. Archive. Sr. M.K.* Beside it in the margin is the small inked figure, a circle with one upright stroke through it, hooked at the foot. Sefa leans over the page from the other side, close enough to see the strokes of the ink.

Hesper takes the questions in order, the way she takes everything.

"The notice is yours." She slides the folded sheet across to you. "The authority I'll write now." She sits for the first time since you came in, takes a clean sheet from the drawer and writes without stopping. She doesn't reach for the rack of stamps. "Those are his. I won't put his seal on my business." She signs it, sands it and hands it to you. It runs four lines: *I, Hesper Vallow, widow and proved heir of Aubrey Vallow, notary of Beregost, authorise the bearer, Bram Halloway, to treat on my behalf with Master Gaspar Thole for the redemption of the coffer named in his notice.* "The will doesn't leave this house unless I go with it. The money will be ready."

Then she turns to your last two questions. She rests her inked hand flat on the desk.

"He was tired. He had been tired since the autumn." That's all she says to the first one, and she lets it stand. "Nobody was with him. He went out before light, to the dawn service. He often did. A novice found him at the foot of the steps when she came to sweep. The temple's healer laid him out. She wrote that he fell."

When Sefa says the notice blames a lost ticket, Hesper shakes her head once. "It doesn't say the ticket is lost. It doesn't say where the ticket is at all. That's my word, not his." She turns the day-book a little toward Sefa. "And the mark isn't beside Thole. He wrote *G.T.* and the hour, and nothing else. The mark is beside the temple." She pauses. "Sister Kell keeps the archive, not the court. Ask her whatever you like. But whatever she writes down goes into the temple's books."

She watches Pell set the purse in the middle of the desk. "Then it's agreed. The fifty is yours to divide as you see fit." She leaves it lying where he put it.

To the idea of walking into Thole's with one of you beside her: "I'll go. He has seen me twice. He hasn't seen me with company." Something in her face goes harder. "I would like to see him not open the door to a man in mail."

Last, the yard. "There's a door in the back wall, under the pear tree. It's bolted on this side and hasn't been opened since the winter. It gives onto the cart alley behind the smithies. The alley runs up behind the cooper's yard and comes out on the main street two doors below the trough." She stands. "I can be ready to go to Thole in a quarter of an hour. Tell me which of you is coming, and whether we go now or wait until your watcher has gone."

*(Out of game: your two questions and your lawful-route plan were honest talk, so they needed no roll. Sister Maudra is your fallback if Thole refuses, so nothing happens there until the group goes to the temple.)*

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Hesper's letter of authority; + Thole's courtesy notice

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: The coffer stays shut

Where you are: Aubrey Vallow's study, at the desk · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa looks up from the mark and folds her arms. She doesn't reach for the purse. "The hand that drew this was copying something seen, not remembered. Slow strokes, made with care. A sign of a thing, not a word. If that is meant to point anywhere, the original may be somewhere a person could stand and look at it—a wall, a gate, a step. The route to the temple, maybe, or the tabernacle door." She pauses. "Have you seen this figure anywhere before? Not written. Drawn, scratched, marked on stone or wood?"

She meets Hesper's eye. "I'll walk in with you to Thole. Not before him, not behind. He has refused a widow twice. Let him see you don't come alone this time." A beat. "But I agree with Pell. Three people at your front door in daylight will draw the watcher like a candle. Let Pell go over the yard wall first. Then we go out the back together, by the cart alley, and meet him on the main street."

She looks from you to Pell. "If Thole opens the door to Hesper and a man in mail beside her, I'll be the one watching his face while she speaks. When he refuses—if he refuses—let his clerk look out the window and see we still don't leave." She pauses. "And ask around who Corwen Ashby is before we go. If Thole sees his buyer in the street, or we do, that changes the walk."

She moves toward the back door, then turns. "But Pell, if the tiefling flinched and is still by the trough, ask him if he's hired, and by whom. That's faster than following him."

Pell takes the fifty and counts it out on the desk in three piles: seventeen, seventeen, sixteen. He leaves the two larger piles on the wood in front of you and Sefa and pockets the smallest without comment. Hesper watches him do it and says nothing.

"Go now," he tells Hesper. "Don't wait for him to leave. I want him to see you walk down that lane with Bram beside you. If he's only watching the house, he'll stay put. If he's watching for the coffer, he'll run to whoever pays him the moment you turn toward Thole's. Either way, I'll learn something."

He looks at you. "Give me a count of a hundred before you open the front door. I'll be in the alley by then. Walk slowly, and don't look at the corner. Let him have a good look at you."

To Sefa: "Your choice. Thole's with them, or the temple. If you go to Sister Kell, don't show her the mark first. Ask about Aubrey's visits and watch how she answers. Then show her." He touches something inside his coat. "I'll keep my copy, so we've each got one if you want to draw your own. Whatever she writes down goes in their books, so tell her as little as you can."

He looks around at all three of you. "Thole's front step, or the cooper's corner, at noon. Whoever isn't there by the bell, the rest go looking." Then he goes out to the yard.

Hesper listens to you with her eyes on the folded papers as they go into your pack. "Give me a quarter of an hour. The will is upstairs, and so is the money." She says nothing about the sword belt. Her eyes drop to it once and come back up.

She answers Sefa's question at once. "No. Not drawn, not cut, not anywhere. I would remember." She looks at the day-book a moment longer. "And Ashby isn't in either book. I looked for him the day the notice came." When Sefa suggests the alley, Hesper shakes her head once. "I've gone out by that front door every day for twenty-two years. I'm not leaving my own house by the cart alley to go and pay a debt." Then, a little less flatly, to Sefa: "Come with me. I'd be glad of it."

She goes up the stairs, and you hear a floorboard and a drawer overhead.

After a while the floorboard creaks again, and Hesper comes down. She has a dark cloak over the grey coat. She carries a leather document case under one arm and a drawstring purse in her hand, and she holds the purse the way people hold money they can't spare. "The will, the proving, and a hundred and twenty," she says. "Counted twice." She goes down the hall to the front door and puts her hand on the bar, but she doesn't lift it. It's a little past nine. She waits for you and Sefa.

Where you are: Hesper's front hall, at the barred door · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa follows Hesper into the hall and stands a step behind her, nearer the wall than the door.

"I'll go with her," she says, as if it were never in doubt. Then, lower: "When we come out, I'll walk on her far side from the trough and watch the lane as if I were looking for the morning cart. If he turns to follow, I'll see him."

She looks back at the desk, where her pile of silver and gold still lies. "Leave my share where it is. If we come back with the coffer, then I've earned it."

Then she falls quiet and waits by the bar.

Hesper lifts the bar herself. She lays it against the wall, opens the door onto the bright lane and steps out without looking toward the corner. You come out at her right shoulder, your seventeen gold in your purse. Sefa takes the far side, away from the trough, and turns her head down the lane as if she were waiting for the morning cart. Behind you the study is empty. Sefa's seventeen gold lies on the dead man's desk where she left it.

You walk up the lane at Hesper's pace, which is quick and even. The coal cart has finished at the smithy yard. Hammers ring on both sides of you.

You watch the corner ahead the way you'd watch a ford before the wagons go in. You look at the doorways, the shade and the people sitting still. The tiefling in the cooper's doorway sees a man in mail coming and steps down off the step to make room. He ducks his head the way people do when they're used to being looked at. He doesn't watch you pass.

The stable lad does watch you, the way anyone watches a man in mail. Then his eyes go back to the carts. You spent ten years in coaching yards, and something about the boy doesn't fit. It's an hour past the bell. At that hour every lad in every inn yard on the Way is mucking out or hauling water, and this one sits on a trough with no horse, no bucket and no fork. Either he's skiving and doesn't care who sees it, or someone is paying him to sit there.

You turn onto the main street. Sefa looks back once at the turn, casually, like a woman checking for traffic. The main street is full of carts, and the doorways are full of people with their own business.

Thole's house stands on the main street, five doors past the cooper's, on the side toward the temple. It's narrow and stone-faced, with a brass-bound door and a small barred grille at head height. A painted board over the lintel reads *G. THOLE, LOANS ON SURETY*. Hesper knocks twice.

The grille opens. A pair of pale eyes looks out at Hesper, then at your shield and mail, then past all three of you at the street. Nobody says anything for a while. Then a bolt slides back, then a second one, and the door opens.

Gaspar Thole is a soft, careful man of fifty in a good brown coat, his sparse hair combed flat. He lets you into a front room with a counter across it. On the counter there's a brass rail, a pair of money scales, and a big ledger lying open. At the back of the room, behind the counter, there's a second door. It's iron, painted dark green, with a keyhole the size of a thumb. Thole bolts the street door behind you before he says a word.

"Mistress Vallow." He goes behind the counter, which puts the brass rail between you. "You've brought company."

Hesper stops at the counter. She sets her document case on it, puts the drawstring purse beside the case, and rests her inked hand flat on the wood. "One hundred and twenty gold. The will and its proving. Master Halloway holds my written authority. I've come to redeem my husband's pledge."

Thole looks at the purse without touching it. He turns the ledger round on the counter so it faces you and puts a finger on an entry. The writing is the same careful hand as the notice: *Coffer, iron, banded, hasp sealed in yellow wax, A. Vallow, 120 gp, eight months.* Under it is a clause copied out in full: *redeemable until sundown of the term by the bearer of my ticket, or my lawful heir producing it.* His thumb rests on the next line down and stays there.

Sefa meets the old woman's eyes without glancing at the drawing first.

"No, Sister. Not on stone, not on wood, not in wax—so far. We asked the widow before we came up the hill, and she said the same: in twenty-two years she's never seen it anywhere in that house. We've seen it once, in Aubrey's day-book, beside his last visit to you. I haven't seen it since."

Maudra hears you out with her fingertips on the table's edge. At *yellow wax* her fingers press down on the wood until the knuckles go pale. She waits until you have asked your question, and then a little longer.

"Yellow." She says it to the drawing, not to you. "Not red."

She turns to Sefa, hears her through to the end, and gives her a short nod. "Here first. That was right."

Then she leaves the table. She goes down the long room to a press at the far end, a tall cupboard of black oak with no lock on it, and comes back with a thin book bound in boards covered in faded saffron cloth. It's no bigger than a psalter. She doesn't open it at once. She sets it on the table beside the chained rolls and keeps her palm on the cover.

"You asked me plainly, Master Halloway, so I'll answer you the same way. Yes. He asked me about a seal." She opens the book. "This house made four of them, two hundred years ago, for the dawn office. When two merchant houses swore a bargain here, the oath went under one of these. Wax the colour of first light." Her finger rests on the page. "This is the register of them."

There are four drawings on the open page, done in brown ink by a careful hand much older than Aubrey's. Each one is a circle split by an upright key, the same figure as your scrap. They aren't all the same, though. Each key has a different foot: a plain bar on the first, a split on the second, a ring on the third. The fourth ends in a small hook. A line of tiny letters in an old, formal script runs round each rim. Under all four, in a different and later ink, someone has written a single entry: *Lost, all four, in the fire of the chapter house. Year of the Bright Blade.* That was ninety years ago.

"The hook," Maudra says. "That's the fourth. Aubrey drew it from the thing itself, not from this page. I showed him this page afterwards, and he went white." She closes the book. "The register says it burned. So either the register is wrong, or someone took it out of this house before the fire and kept quiet about it for ninety years."

She doesn't sit down.

"He asked me how one is opened. I'll tell you what I told him. It isn't broken. It's opened, by the hand it was set for. Any other hand, and what lies under it is gone. Burnt to nothing inside the box, and the box still shut." Her voice stays brisk, but it's quieter now. "Whose hand that one was set for, he didn't tell me. I didn't ask. I thought there would be time."

She looks at you, then at Sefa, and this time she holds your eyes.

"So now I owe two things. One is to a dead man, who left me something for his widow. The other is to this house, which has a seal sitting on a moneylender's shelf that by its own register burned before I was born." She lays her hand flat on the saffron boards. "I mean to keep both, if I can."

"Bring me her two lines, and I'll do what he asked of me. But when that coffer comes out of Thole's, I'll want to see that wax with my own eyes before anyone carries it further. Here, or on her own step. I don't mind which." A pause. "Will she allow that? Or must I go to Brother Lucan instead and tell him what's sitting at Thole's?"

Below the high windows the cloister is quiet. Somewhere in the garden the bean-row brother is humming.

Then she puts her hand on the doorframe.

"So. You have the ticket, and the court will have it in an hour, and Thole before sundown." She says it like an entry in the catalogue. "Then the coffer goes to her step. And how am I to know when it's on her step, Master Halloway? I won't wait in the square for it. Do I come down with you now, or will one of you climb my stair again to fetch me?"

*(Out of game: correction accepted. You and Sefa reach Maudra at about five past one.)*

Your records, changed:
Carried: − Hesper's two lines to Sister Maudra

Where you are: At Sister Maudra's archive door, top of the chapter house stair · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sefa takes the folded paper from Sister Maudra with both hands, carefully, and doesn't open it until Maudra says she may. When she sees the ticket inside, she lets out a slow breath and reads it twice.

"The whole blessed thing hinges on this," she says quietly. "And he left it with you, not in the house. He knew Thole's terms better than anyone."

She folds it again along Aubrey's creases and tucks it into an inner pocket.

"Brother Lucan goes first, before Thole touches it." She glances at you. "If the wheelwright takes an hour, we use it. We sit in the antechamber and wait our turn, and we keep hold of the ticket until the warden has seen it and put his ruling under the court's seal. Thole only gets what the undertaking promises, the full sum and the coffer across his counter, after the law has spoken."

Then she turns back to Maudra, and her voice softens.

"We'll send for you, Sister, not leave you standing in the square. When we have the coffer out of Thole's, one of us will come up your stair or send Brother Teo to knock." She pauses. "But I'd rather you weren't waiting alone at Hesper's door with a crowd forming. If the time comes late and the street gets long shadows, meet us at the back, Hesper's yard door, under the pear tree. She'll allow you in that way, and no one on the lane will have a seat for it."

She holds the old woman's eyes. "You said you'd keep both debts. So will we. Her step, her barred door, her husband's seal. All of it."

Sister Maudra watches the ticket go into Sefa's pocket and doesn't comment.

She answers you first.

"Come down with you now. To Lucan's table, then a moneylender's counter, then the main street." She repeats it back to you like a list of shelf-marks, and her tone makes it plain what she thinks of the list. "A sister of this house walking into Gaspar Thole's behind a man in mail. By the evening office every forge in Beregost would have it that the temple had come to take a widow's box away from her. No, Master Halloway."

When Sefa offers her the yard door under the pear tree, the old woman goes quiet for a moment.

"Her step, she said." Maudra considers it. "Her back step is as much hers as her front one, and nobody sits on a trough to watch it." She gives a short nod. "The yard, then. When it's out of Thole's and on its way to her, send Brother Teo up my stair. I'll come round by the garden and the forge boys' path. I walked it when I was young enough to be scolded for it." She doesn't say how long ago that was. "I'll be slower than you. Don't take it inside before I get there."

She hears what Sefa says last, about keeping both debts, all of it, and for a moment she just looks at her.

"See that you do, Mistress."

On Pell she doesn't need telling twice. "Dunmore. If anyone comes asking under that name, Teo will tell him you've gone to Lucan and then to Thole's, and then to the widow." She puts her hand on the door. "Go on. You've less afternoon than you think."

The iron-bound door shuts behind you before you reach the second step.

Brother Teo is at the bottom of the stair, and he follows you back along the east walk without being asked. The antechamber is cool and dim. The wheelwright's voice is still rising and falling behind the inner door, something about a hub and whether a spoke counts as a fault if it only cracked once it was on the road. Teo sits down at his table, finds your line in the book and writes a second one under it in his small upright hand: *Bram Halloway, again. The ticket.* He sands it and adds Maudra's message for Pell in the margin below.

"After the wheelwright," he says. "He's nearly done. He's started saying the same things twice."

He turns out to be right. You wait a little under half an hour on the bench. The slab of light from the high window creeps across the floor, and nobody comes in from the square. Then the inner door opens, and a big man with sawdust in his beard comes out, still arguing over his shoulder. Brother Lucan stands in the doorway behind him. He sees you and Sefa on the bench and lifts his eyebrows a fraction.

"That was quick," he says. "Come in."

He sits down at the long table and holds out his hand, as he did this morning. Sefa takes Aubrey's folded paper from her pocket and opens it on the table herself. She doesn't let go of the card until his fingers are on it.

Lucan reads the outside first, *For my widow, if it comes to it. A.V.*, and says the initials quietly to the page. Then he reads the ticket, once quickly and once slowly with a finger under the lines. The finger stops on *the hasp sealed in yellow* and stays there a moment longer than the words need. He says nothing about it. He moves on to *No. 41. G. Thole*, takes down a red-bound book from the shelf behind him, finds a page and runs his finger down a column.

"Thole registers his ticket numbers with this court every quarter, so nobody can forge them. Forty-one, issued in the month Aubrey's day-book gives." He closes the book and squares the card in front of him with two fingers. "It's real."

He leans back.

"You understand what you're holding? *By the bearer of my ticket.* Mistress Marrin is the bearer, sent by the heir. Thole's own terms require him to take a hundred and twenty from her across his counter, and he doesn't need a word from me to do it." He taps Thole's undertaking, which you have laid beside the ticket. "He asked for my seal because he had no ticket in front of him. Now there is one."

"Even so, I'll write it if you want it. A ruling that the heir's redemption, made by her bearer with this ticket, ends every other claim on the coffer, Master Ashby's included, from the moment the money is paid. Thole can show it to anyone who comes knocking afterwards, and so can she." He folds his ink-stained hands on the table. "Two gold. It goes in the book under the pledge, with you as applicant, Master Halloway. Do you want it, or will you take the ticket to Thole as it is?"

Through the window behind him the bean-row brother has started on the far poles. It's getting on for twenty to two.

*(Out of game: no rolls this round. Maudra made her own choice, and Lucan checked the ticket against the court's own register.)*

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Maudra sees the wax at the yard door

Where you are: Brother Lucan's hearing room, temple · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sefa doesn't hesitate.

"Take the ruling." She says it quietly, but with the certainty of someone closing a door on a draught. "The ticket makes Thole take our money. The seal makes every man behind us—Ashby, a later ticket-bearer, anyone with a long face and a short memory—argue with the temple instead of with Hesper. At two gold, that's cheap armour for the walk home."

She glances at the ticket still under the warden's fingers, then at you. "Once it's paid and the coffer leaves Thole's counter, the street won't care which of them was right. I'd rather we carry the court's voice with us than have to explain a moneylender's clause to a crowd."

She sits back a little. "Let Brother Lucan write it while the room is still ours."

Brother Lucan looks at the two gold pieces on the table and leaves them where you put them while he hears the rest.

"Applicant, Bram Halloway. Under the pledge of A. Vallow, deceased, to G. Thole." He takes a sheet from the drawer, a heavier stock than the petition book's, and uncaps his ink. "A receipt as well. You'll have both."

He writes slowly in a small, upright court hand and doesn't stop to think. Sefa makes her case for the seal while he writes. He doesn't look up, but at *argue with the temple instead of with Hesper* the pen pauses for half a word and then goes on. When he's done, he turns the sheet round on the table for you both to read:

*Court of contracts of the Song of the Morning. On the application of Bram Halloway, under the pledge of A. Vallow, deceased, to G. Thole, lender on surety. The court has seen ticket No. 41 in the lender's hand, entered in this court's register of his tickets. It rules: redemption of the coffer named therein, made before sundown of the term by the bearer of that ticket, sent by the lawful heir and proved here in the spring, ends the pledge and every other claim on the coffer from the moment the sum is paid, including any claim of purchase by Master Corwen Ashby or any other. L. Pryce, warden.*

He sands it and takes a small box down from the shelf behind him. It's plain wood, and inside is a brass seal with a rayed sun. He warms a stick of saffron wax at the candle, lets a coin-sized pool fall at the foot of the sheet, and presses the sun into it. He holds it there for a breath, then lifts it. The rays come up clean.

The receipt takes him less time: *Received of Bram Halloway, two gold pieces, the court's fee for a ruling under the pledge of A. Vallow. L. Pryce.* He sweeps the two coins into a drawer and slides the receipt across after the ruling. Then he picks up ticket No. 41, folds it back into Aubrey's paper along its old creases, and gives it to Sefa rather than you.

"The bearer carries the ticket," he says. "Keep it that way until it's on Thole's counter."

Then he gets to your last question. He puts his hand flat on the court book while he answers.

"If Gaspar Thole sees that seal and still won't take a lawful redemption, come back to this room before the bell. I'll send Brother Teo to his door with a summons, and he'll stand in that chair and explain himself to me. A lender in Beregost who defies this court's seal lends to nobody for long, and he knows it." He takes his hand off the book. "He won't refuse. He asked for this. What he'll do is read it twice, wipe his palms, and look at his door."

He squares the court book on the shelf with two fingers and sits back.

"I'll want to hear when it's done, Master Halloway. Before the square does."

The sheet with the court's sun on it lies on the table in front of you, still warm at the foot. Outside the window the bean-row brother has worked his way down to the far poles. It's a little before two o'clock. Hesper's door is the length of the main street away, and Thole's is on the way there.

Your records, changed:
Money: + 38 gp; − 40 gp
Carried: + Lucan's receipt for the court's fee; + Sealed ruling of the court of contracts

Where you are: the warden's court of contracts room, Song of the Morning temple, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sefa takes Aubrey's folded ticket back with both hands, tucks it into her inner pocket and presses it flat with her palm.

"Then we're as armed as we're going to be." She nods once to Brother Lucan. "The court will hear it's done before the square does. I'd sooner carry that news myself than let a carter bring it."

The warden looks up at her. "So would I, Mistress." He's already reaching for the next blank sheet. "A carter tells it wrong, and then I have to hear it twice."

Brother Lucan watches you leave the ruling flat on the table until the saffron wax has gone from glossy to dull. Only then do you slide it into your pack between the undertaking and the notice, where the stiff sheets on either side will keep it from bending. The receipt goes in after it.

Sefa waits until you have the ruling and receipt secure, then moves toward the door. "Hesper's first. The money, and we tell her about the yard. She hasn't signed up to unbar the back for anyone yet, and it's her door, not ours. If Pell has come back while we were up here, all the better. If he hasn't, we leave her word that we've gone to Thole."

That's the end of it. The warden doesn't get up. The inner door swings half shut behind you.

Sefa glances down the antechamber as if measuring the light. "Then Thole, while the seal's fresh and the day still has teeth. Main street, not the footway. Let anyone watching see a man in mail and a woman with the temple's sun in her pocket, not two furtive figures down the back."

You're halfway across the antechamber when Brother Teo looks up from his pens. He was waiting for you, and he puts a finger on his book before you reach the propped door.

"Master Halloway. There's word for you." He turns the book around. Under your two lines, in the same small upright hand, is a third: *Pell Dunmore, for Master Halloway.* Below it Teo has written the message. "He came in while you were with the warden, a quarter of an hour ago, maybe a little less. Lean, quick, grit on his knees. I told him you were inside. I don't interrupt the warden, so he left this." Teo reads it out exactly, the way a clerk does: "*That I'm here, and that I'll meet them at the garden wicket on the east lane, not out front. He'll know why.*" He looks up. "He said something about a cart to catch as well. Then he went out by the square door and turned left along the wall."

Maudra's message for Pell is still in the margin next to it, written before he ever arrived.

Through the propped door the square is bright and nearly empty in the early afternoon. The great steps rise on the right. Past them, down the main street and too far off to see a face, is the alehouse bench. You have seen a big man sprawled on it before. Left along the chapter house wall, in its strip of shade, is the buttress at the corner and the east lane behind it, where you and Sefa came out of the footway an hour ago. From the wicket that footway runs behind the houses all the way to the cooper's yard and the cart alley.

It's a little before two.

Where you are: chapter house antechamber, by Teo's desk near the propped square door · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sefa nods once and turns toward the square door, not the propped front.

"The wicket, then. Left along the wall, in the temple's shade. He didn't choose that corner for the cool." She keeps her voice low under the antechamber's hush. "Whatever cart he means, I'd rather hear it from his mouth than from a crier in the square."

She stops just inside the oak door and glances back at you. "He said *not out front*, so we don't step out side by side and make a procession. You first, I'll be two paces behind, like a man going about his business and a woman keeping to the shade. We're not running. We want to look like people with time, not people with a sealed court ruling in their satchel."

Her hand goes to the pocket where the ticket rests, then falls back to her side.

"From the wicket we'll learn what he's seen. Then Hesper's. Whether that means the main street or the footway depends on what he tells us."

Brother Teo nods at your thanks as if it were part of the job, and maybe it is. He's already sanding a line in his book before you turn away.

Sefa lets you step out first and follows two paces behind you, keeping to the shade.

The square is bright and quiet in the early afternoon. Water runs in the fountain with nobody at it. You turn left at once and keep close to the chapter house wall, where the temple's shadow runs in a strip about an arm wide. You walk at the pace of a man with an errand but no hurry. Sefa comes behind you at the same pace, one hand loose at her side, looking like a woman who happens to be going the same way.

The great steps rise on your right. For a few strides before the steps cut it off, the main street opens up between the last roofs, all the way down to the alehouse hatch. The big man is still on the end of the bench with his legs out across the cobbles and a cup at his elbow, too far off to see his face. His head is turned toward the foot of the steps and the square in front of them. It isn't turned toward the strip of shade along the wall. Then the steps come between you and him, and there's only rose granite on your right and whitewash on your left.

Nobody calls out, and no one in the square looks your way twice.

At the buttress on the corner the wall turns, and you step out of the square into the east lane. The sheds are on one side. On the other is the long garden wall with its plank wicket and the latch-string hanging through its hole. Across the lane, between the two woodstores, is the narrow mouth of the footway you and Sefa came out of an hour ago. Over the wall the bean poles stand in their pairs, and a brother in a straw hat is bent over the far rows with his back to the cloister. It's a few minutes past two.

*(Out of game: under the retcon we agreed, Pell is waiting by this wicket at about 14:03, so your threads meet here. Your words to him will be heard when his player answers next round, in the joined scene.)*

Where you are: east lane, by the garden wicket · Time: Day 1 · evening

Pell comes off the garden wall as you round the buttress. He meets you halfway down the lane, so the three of you stop in the shed's shadow with the corner of the temple between you and the square. The plank wicket is a few steps behind him. Across the ruts is the gap between the two woodstores. From down here it's only a dark slot between stacked logs.

Sefa comes up at the same even pace without raising a hand. Her eyes go to the coal grit on Pell's knees and the tar on his coat before they go to his face. She stops close enough to speak low.

"Pell. You've been down, then up. Tell us where—and what cart you meant. We have the day by the throat, but we've been bright about it, not quiet."

She glances once over her shoulder toward the square, then back. "Bram has a sealed ruling from the temple, and I'm carrying the ticket itself. Sister Maudra found it for us. So if that cart can wait, we go to Hesper's now; if it can't, we hear about it before we step back out in front of any man on a bench."

Pell keeps his voice low and gives it to you short.

"Don't go back out front. Ashby's big sunburnt man is on the alehouse bench across from Thole's with a cup. He can see Thole's door, the street both ways and the foot of the great steps. He's been there since noon and he doesn't care who sees him." He glances past your shoulder toward the corner. "Did you come round the front of the steps just now, or along the chapter house wall?"

He doesn't wait long for the answer.

"Short version of my morning. The watcher's a stable lad at the Red Sheaf, north end. A man in a grey riding cloak pays him silver at the noon bell to tell what he saw. The lad told him three of you went out, a shield and two women, and which way you turned. The chandler across the street has the man on his slate in his own hand as *Ashby & Corve*, an iron buyer, there near a tenday. He has two hired swords. The big one's on that bench. A thin one rides out before light and comes back after dark." A beat. "And yesterday Ashby bought two flasks of good lamp oil and a new tinderbox. I don't like that, with a sealed box he's meant to be buying."

He nods back toward the chapter house.

"Hesper told me Thole's terms: no money without a ticket, unless the court of contracts gives him a sealed writing that the heir's redemption ends it. Teo told me the warden sent you up to Sister Maudra before noon, and that's all I know." He looks from you to Sefa. "So. Does the court give the writing? What did the archivist want with you? And how long have we got before the warden stops hearing?"

He tips his head at the gap between the woodstores across the lane.

"That path runs west behind the houses, toward the cooper's end. I haven't walked it yet. If we're carrying anything out of Thole's later, I'd rather bring it back that way than past the bench."

He doesn't say a word about the cart.

Over the wall the old brother in the straw hat has straightened up between two bean poles. He watches the three of you muttering beside his gate the way a man watches weather coming. Nobody looks back at him. After a moment he sniffs, bends again and goes on pinching blackfly into his clay pot.

Nobody else is in the lane. The cat on the shed roofs has its eyes shut. From the square round the corner comes the sound of the fountain, and nothing else. It's a few minutes past two, and Pell is waiting for answers.

*(Out of game: there was nothing uncertain in a question to a friend, so no roll. Pell answered about the watcher, the Red Sheaf, Ashby & Corve and the oil, but he said nothing about the cart.)*

Where you are: shed's shadow, lane behind the temple · Time: Day 1 · evening

The session is over.

How was the table?
Was there something you wanted to do and didn't?
Who did you take the other two players to be?

messages.text:
I glance up the lane where Hesper is looking, then step inside first, keeping my sword sheathed. I move clear of the doorway so Sefa and Pell can follow.

“Best talk away from the street, then. What needs doing by nightfall—and who are you watching for?”

I leave the purse where it is.

“Is that fifty our advance, or the money to redeem the pledge? How much does Thole say he's owed—and have you papers showing your right to collect it?”

I glance at the dusty seal-stamps, then back to her.

“I can agree to leave it shut. But before we take your coin: what do you know of what's inside, and has anyone besides your husband warned you against opening it? If there's danger in carrying it, we need to know.”

“What have you found, Pell?”

I step beside the desk to look at the entry and the unfamiliar mark without disturbing the pages.

“Mistress Vallow, we'll try the lawful road first. We'll need that notice, your proved copy of the will, and your written authority to act for you. Keep the redemption money ready until we know whether Thole will accept it without the ticket.”

I glance toward Sefa and Pell. “If he won't, we find out precisely why. Sister Maudra may be able to help us after that.”

Then I turn back to Hesper. “One other thing. Did Aubrey seem hurt or frightened when he told you to keep it shut? And was anyone with him when he fell?”

“I'll walk with you, Mistress Vallow. Bring the will and the redemption money. We go when you're ready—no sense letting the morning slip.”

I fold the authority and notice carefully into my pack.

“Pell, we'll give you those fifteen minutes to get into place. I won't hail you if I spot you. Mind yourself; we don't yet know that either fellow is watching this house.”

I turn to Sefa. “I'd welcome you beside us at Thole's. Another pair of ears may be worth more than the mail.”

While Hesper gets ready, I loosen my sword belt a notch so the hilt sits comfortably, keeping the blade sheathed. “We're going to offer payment, not threaten him. Let him give us his answer plainly.”

I pocket my seventeen gold and join Hesper at the door.

“Ready. You lead us to his shop; I'll stay beside you.”

Once Sefa is with us, I let Hesper lift the bar and step out with her. I keep an easy pace, giving the corner no deliberate look, and leave my sword alone. On the walk I watch the people and doorways ahead, as I would with a wagon to escort.

“Then let's keep to the writing,” I say evenly. “May we see the rest of that entry, beneath your thumb?”

I stay beside Hesper, hands clear of my sword.

“You're right that a missing ticket leaves a claim unsettled. But how does three hundred gold settle it where a hundred and twenty won't? Would you give her a written release against any later bearer?”

I pause. “And is there a lawful way to cancel the missing ticket before sundown—a declaration before the temple court, or a surety? We'd rather pay for that than buy the same coffer twice.”

“Mine can,” I tell Hesper. “I'll ask for a ruling on the clause as written, without naming you. If they require your name, I'll stop and come back to you.”

I turn to Thole. “Put that offer in writing, please: a ruling under the temple seal that the heir's redemption ends the ticket, delivered before sundown, and you'll release the coffer for one hundred and twenty. Copy the exact clause beneath it. Sign it.”

My voice stays matter-of-fact. “That way we bring back what you need, rather than spend the afternoon misunderstanding each other.”

To Hesper, I add, “Keep your money and papers with you for now. We should meet Pell outside before going to the Song.”

I read the undertaking through, then fold it carefully into my pack.

“Thank you. The door, please, Master Thole.”

Once we're outside, I speak quietly to Hesper and Sefa. “We'll walk you home first. It's barely a detour, and you have the redemption money on you.”

On the walk, I ask Hesper, “The undertaking names Aubrey. May I show it to the warden, provided I neither name you nor present your authority? I don't want to keep the letter of our promise and break its meaning.”

I glance to Sefa. “Then the chapter house, if you're willing. We'll return here by noon for Pell.”

I wait until the bar settles, then turn toward the main street with Sefa.

“The tiefling was waiting for wages. Saw his tally match the cooper's. The boy's still idle at the trough, though. We'll tell Pell when we meet him.”

I keep my voice low as we walk. “At the court, I'll show Thole's undertaking and ask whether they can give the ruling it requires. No authority letter, no petition in Hesper's name.”

I head for the chapter house door to the left of the temple steps. Once inside, I approach whoever receives petitioners.

“Bram Halloway. I'd like to speak with the warden of contracts about a pledge that falls due at sundown. The lender has put the question in writing.”

“Master Corwen Ashby. Thole says he's offered two hundred and fifty gold, payable at sundown. He hasn't asked Thole about a ticket. That's all we know of his claim.”

I leave the undertaking on the table.

“Thole first asked three hundred to release the coffer without the ticket. Then he agreed to the original hundred and twenty if we brought your ruling. He seemed concerned about the buyer as well as any later bearer.”

I take out two gold pieces, but pause before setting them down.

“I can pay the fee. First, I need to be clear: I'm asking in my own name, on this undertaking. Would the entry name only Aubrey's pledge and me as applicant, without entering his widow as a petitioner?”

“No. His widow searched his papers and found no ticket. We hoped the clause offered a lawful way without it. You've made that plain.”

I put the coins away and take back Thole's undertaking.

“His day-book records visits to your archive—‘Song. Archive. Sr. M.K.’ There's an unfamiliar mark beside one: a circle pierced by an upright stroke, hooked at the foot. Does that mean anything to you?”

I pause. “We'd like to speak with Sister Maudra Kell about those visits. Can you direct us to her?”

“She hired us to recover the coffer, yes. I went to Lucan on my own application, after Thole offered to release it if the court approved redemption without the ticket. Lucan couldn't approve it.”

I keep my voice low in the quiet cloister.

“We're looking for the ticket now. Aubrey's day-book records two visits to your archive. We'd like to know what he came to consult, and whether he left anything in your keeping.”

I leave the drawing in my pack for now.

“I have her letter, in her own hand. But it authorises me to treat with Thole—not to collect anything from you. I won't claim it says more than it does.”

I take out the letter and offer it for her to read.

“If you need her word addressed to you, I'll go back and ask her for it.”

Then I bring out my drawing of the mark and hold it where Maudra can see.

“This is as near as I remember it. Pell made a copy directly from the day-book; he has that one.”

“No. Only in the day-book, and our copies of it.”

I glance at Sefa, leaving her to answer for herself.

“Thole's notice describes yellow wax sealing the coffer's hasp. We haven't seen the coffer, and the notice names no mark on the seal. Hesper said Aubrey always used red.”

I look back to Maudra. “Is that what he asked you about—a seal?”

“I'll ask her. I can't give her leave for her, but looking at the wax on her own step seems a fair request. We've promised the coffer stays shut. Your warning gives us better reason to keep that promise.”

I return the authority letter to my pack.

“Please give us time to bring her answer before you go to Lucan. We'll tell her exactly what you've told us, and ask for the two lines naming you and whoever she sends.”

I pause before turning to leave. “One thing for carrying it safely: can touching the wax trigger it, or only trying to open it?”

“Pell first. He's expecting us.”

I head out through the antechamber toward Thole's, keeping a brisk walk with Sefa rather than running through the square. I look for Pell at the lender's step, then the cooper's corner.

If we find him, I draw close enough to speak privately. “The court needs the ticket. Maudra has something Aubrey left for Hesper, but needs Hesper's written leave to hand it over. We're going to fetch that now. What did you learn?”

“He said we'd go looking. Let's start where he left the house.”

I turn to Sefa. “Stay together. We'll ask Hesper if he's returned, get Maudra's letter, then check the cart alley.”

I walk down to Hesper's door and knock, standing where she can see me when she opens it.

“Bram and Sefa. Has Pell been back? He missed our noon meeting.”

Once we're inside, I keep it brief. “Maudra says Aubrey left something with her for you. She'll release it to someone carrying two lines in your hand, addressed to her, naming who you send to collect it.”

“And she recognised the mark. It's an old temple seal. She asks to inspect the wax on your own doorstep when we bring the coffer—not open it. Will you allow that?”

“Thank you. We'll give Maudra your terms exactly.”

I turn to Sefa. “I'll check the yard and cart alley; you take the front street and temple side, as you suggested. Meet at the trough in half an hour. If either of us finds trouble, call for help rather than going into it alone.”

I go out into Hesper's yard and examine the back door before opening it: bolt, latch, and ground around the threshold. Then I follow Pell's route into the cart alley, looking for anything dropped, signs of a struggle, or somewhere a man might be lying out of sight.

If anyone is working along the alley, I ask whether they've seen Pell, describing his clothes and healer's satchel. I keep my sword sheathed and my ears open between the hammer strokes.

I point out the scuffed butt and flattened moss to Sefa.

“Looks like his perch. Clear view of the trough, and he came down without a struggle. If he followed the boy, this is where he'd have started.”

I look toward the narrow footway. “Together, then. We'll check this through to the temple end. If there's no sign of him, we take Maudra her letter and ask whether he's been there.”

I lead down the footway at a steady walk, checking the bends and recessed doorways before passing them, listening for voices or movement ahead.

Before we leave the tired boy, I ask, “Seen a lean man in a dark coat pass here today? He carries a healer's satchel. Or a lad about your age, dressed for stable work?”

I don't keep him standing longer than his answer takes.

To Sefa, I say, “No sign of a struggle. He may be following something well beyond these lanes. Let's get Maudra's parcel moving, and ask whether he's called there.”

I head round to the chapter house and the archive by the route we know, with Hesper's letter ready.

? We're going directly to Maudra now, at about one o'clock. Please correct the conflicting chronology rather than delay our arrival to fit another thread.

“Come with us now, if you're able, Sister. We'll wait for Lucan, then go to Thole's and straight to Hesper's step. Better than leaving you uncertain when to come.”

I look to Sefa and the ticket. “That stays safe with you. We have what we need to redeem it.”

To Maudra, I add, “Our missing companion is Pell Dunmore. If he comes asking after us, please have word left that we're taking the lawful route through Lucan and Thole, then back to Hesper.”

I head downstairs with Sefa and ask Brother Teo for the next available hearing.

“We've found the ticket. The warden asked to see it before the lender does. We'll wait our turn.”

“Yes, please. With Ashby's claim expressly covered, as you said.”

I set two gold pieces on the table.

“Enter me as applicant under Aubrey's pledge, as we agreed. We'd also be grateful for a receipt for the fee.”

While he prepares the ruling, I turn quietly to Sefa. “Next stop Hesper's for the redemption money. We should tell her about the yard arrangement before promising it on her behalf. Then Thole.”

Before we leave, I ask Lucan, “If Thole refuses the ticket and payment despite this ruling, whom should we fetch?”

“You'll hear from us when it's done. Thank you, Brother.”

I let the wax cool before packing the ruling where it won't be crushed, then leave with Sefa for Hesper's house.

On the way, I keep an eye out for Pell without lingering at either meeting place. At Hesper's door I knock and identify us.

Once we're inside, I tell her, “We have the ticket Aubrey left for you, and the court's sealed ruling. Thole must accept the hundred and twenty now. Have you heard from Pell?”

I show her the ruling, then add, “Maudra agreed to look without touching. She proposed coming by the footway to your yard instead of the front step. Will you allow that? We still need to send for her when the coffer is on its way.”

“Good. Thank you for keeping his words straight.”

I turn to Sefa. “Let's hear him before we walk out front. He may know who that bench is watching.”

I go left along the chapter house wall toward the east lane and garden wicket, keeping Sefa beside me. When we reach Pell, I keep my voice low.

“We looked for you at noon. Glad you're on your feet. We have Aubrey's ticket and the court's seal; just need Hesper's money. What's this about a cart?”

I stop by the wicket, leaving the footway clear, and lower my voice to Pell.

“We looked for you at noon. Glad you're on your feet. We've got Aubrey's ticket and the court's sealed ruling. Hesper has the redemption money ready at home.”

I glance back toward the corner, then give him my attention.

“What did you find—and what's this cart we need to catch?”

Good table overall: a compelling small-scale mystery, grounded NPCs, and room for Bram to solve problems without drawing his sword.

**What worked**
- Hesper, Thole, Lucan, and Maudra had distinct voices and believable boundaries.
- The ticket, contract wording, and yellow wax rewarded careful questions. Finding the ticket felt earned.
- Bram had useful work as an escort and negotiator, not merely the party’s shield.
- Pell’s investigation produced information that meaningfully changed our plans.

**What needs tightening**
- **Pacing:** repeated travel, recaps, and confirmation of already-agreed plans stretched a morning’s investigation across the whole session. I’d have liked to reach the redemption—or a clear confrontation—before stopping.
- **Chronology:** timestamps contradicted the narration, and another thread’s future initially constrained our present. Accepting the correction was good; synchronising split-party scenes earlier would avoid that.
- **Player agency:** occasionally the narration supplied dialogue or actions for Bram that I hadn’t written. Small connective movements are fine; substantive answers should stay mine.
- **Out-of-game notes:** repeated explanations that ordinary conversation required no roll added clutter. Save those for genuine rules questions.

I’d happily continue. The strongest next session would bring the three players back into a shared scene quickly and let us act on what we’ve learned.

Yes—**actually redeem the coffer and see what happened on the way home**. We’d spent the session earning the ticket and ruling, and I wanted to put them on Thole’s counter, make him honour his promise, and carry the box past Ashby’s watchers. That felt like the payoff we stopped just short of.

I also wanted a little more direct play with Pell and Sefa: compare what we’d learned, disagree if necessary, then commit to a plan together. We finally reached that point at the end.

I wasn’t missing a fight. Bram getting the coffer home without drawing his sword would have been satisfying—provided we got to face the danger and make that choice.

I took them to be **the players controlling Sefa Marrin and Pell Dunmore**, separate from me playing Bram and from the AI game master. I wasn’t given any information about who those players were outside the game, or whether they were humans or other AI agents.

Their messages reached me through the GM’s narration, so I treated their quoted speech and declared actions as their contributions—not as NPC behaviour I could direct.

When I said I wanted “more direct play” with them, I meant more shared scenes where our characters could hear and answer one another, rather than spending most of the session in separate threads.

screens.text:
The session begins.

Beregost is already at work. Hammers ring from the smithies down the lane, a cart rattles past toward the Trade Way, and the last note of Lathander's morning bell fades over the rooftops.

The oak door opens a hand's width, then wider. Hesper Vallow stands in the gap. She is a spare woman in a plain grey coat, ink on two fingers of her right hand. She looks at each of you in turn: Bram with his painted-over shield, you, and Pell. Then her gaze goes past you, up the lane toward the main street, and stays there a moment too long.

"All three of you. Good." Behind her the hall is dim. Every shutter on the ground floor is closed against the sun. "By nightfall, as I said. Not an hour later." She steps back from the threshold and holds the door, but she doesn't explain yet. She is waiting to see who comes in first, or whether anyone has something to ask her out here on the step.

Your records:
Sefa Marrin — Human, warlock 5 (The Celestial — the Lantern; Pact of the Tome), former hospice novice, level 5
HP 38/38 · AC 14 · Speed 30 feet
STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 10 · CHA 18
Skills: Persuasion +7; Arcana +4; Religion +4; Insight +3
Saves: Wisdom saving throw +3 (proficient); Charisma saving throw +7 (proficient); Strength saving throw −1; Dexterity saving throw +2; Constitution saving throw +2; Intelligence saving throw +1
Attacks: Eldritch Blast +7 to hit, two beams, 1d10+4 force each, range 120 feet; Dagger +5 to hit, 1d4+2 piercing, thrown 20/60
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Spell attack +7; spell save DC 15; Pact Magic: two 3rd-level pact slots, recovered only on a short or long rest; Healing Light: a pool of six d6 per long rest; a bonus action spends up to four dice to heal a creature within 60 feet; Pact of the Tome: the Book of Shadows holds three extra cantrips (Guidance, Spare the Dying, Thaumaturgy); Agonizing Blast: +4 to each Eldritch Blast beam's damage; Repelling Blast: a beam that hits pushes the target up to 10 feet away; Eyes of the Rune Keeper: reads all writing

Limits: Two pact slots only, back only after a rest; Light armour; Strength 8 — weak up close; One concentration spell at a time
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Pact slots 2/2; Healing light 6/6
Money: 1 pp; 8 gp; 41 sp; 12 cp
