Pack: Bedroll and Rations; Candle ×2; Tinderbox

Where you are: on the step outside Hesper Vallow's oak door, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram glances up the lane where Hesper was looking, and Pell's eyes follow his a moment later. Bram goes in first, his sword sheathed, and steps to the left of the doorway so the rest of you can follow. "Best talk away from the street, then. What needs doing by nightfall—and who are you watching for?"

Pell takes in the main street and the doorways before he looks back at Hesper and keeps his voice low. "You looked up that lane like you were expecting someone. Worth knowing who, before we hear the rest." He pauses on the threshold and nods at the closed shutters. "And if it's the sort of someone who watches doors, I'd rather we talk in a room without windows to the street."

You come in right behind Bram with your small, unhurried nod. Pell comes last, out of the sun, and stops near the door where he can still see a hand's width of the lane through the gap.

The hall smells of beeswax and cold ashes. Hesper shuts the door, drops the bar, and stands a moment with her palm flat on the oak.

"Someone has stood at the top of the lane three mornings running," she says. "Young, I think. I see him from the upstairs window, and never well. I don't know who he is. I don't know who sends him." She looks at Pell. "You're right about the street. Come through."

She takes you down the hall, past a front room where the furniture sits under dust sheets, to a study at the back. Its one window looks onto a walled yard with a rain barrel and a pear tree. Shelves of bound ledgers cover two walls. A notary's desk sits under the window, tidy and unused, with a rack of seal-stamps and a dish of red wax that has gone dull with dust. Hesper doesn't sit. She stands behind the desk, her inked hand resting on its edge.

"My husband was Aubrey Vallow, notary of this town for twenty years. He died this winter. He fell on the steps of the Song of the Morning." She says it like an entry in a register. "Eight months ago he pledged an iron coffer to a moneylender on the main street, Gaspar Thole. I didn't know until last week, when Thole sent me a courtesy notice as the widow. The term of the pledge ends at sundown today. After that, Thole may sell it, and he has a buyer. A Master Corwen Ashby. I don't know him."

"I have been to Thole twice. The first time he was polite and told me nothing. The second time he didn't open the door."

From a drawer she takes a leather purse and sets it on the desk. It's heavy, and it stays where she put it.

"The terms. I want the coffer brought here, to this room, before sundown. Fifty gold now, a hundred more on delivery. How you get it from Thole is your affair, provided nothing is done that puts my name before the temple court. And one condition, which isn't negotiable." She raises her eyes to each of you in turn. "It comes to me shut. Not opened, not tried, not looked into. Aubrey asked me to keep it shut, and I mean to."

She waits with her hand beside the purse and doesn't push it toward any of you.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Aubrey Vallow's coffer
+ Quest: Aubrey Vallow's coffer

Where you are: Hesper's back study · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram leaves the purse where it is. "Is that fifty our advance, or the money to redeem the pledge? How much does Thole say he's owed—and have you papers showing your right to collect it?" He glances at the dusty seal-stamps, then back to her. "I can agree to leave it shut. But before we take your coin: what do you know of what's inside, and has anyone besides your husband warned you against opening it? If there's danger in carrying it, we need to know."

Pell doesn't reach for the purse. He glances back down the hall toward the barred door, then at Hesper. "Your watcher might have company. There's a tiefling in a road coat in the cooper's doorway, across from the trough. He turned away when I looked at him, quicker than a man with nothing to hide. The stable lad didn't turn at all. So either one of them is yours, or there are two of them." He shrugs. "Worth knowing before we walk out of here carrying anything."

He nods at the shelves of ledgers. "Here's the part I care about. A pledge has a price to buy it back. What did Aubrey borrow against it, and what does Thole want by sundown? If you can just pay it, the easiest way to get your coffer is to walk in the front door with the money, and nobody goes near a temple court. And a notary of twenty years doesn't pledge anything without writing it down. Did he keep his copy of the contract? The pledge note, a receipt, a ledger entry with Thole's name on it? If that paper's in this room, it's worth more to us than any lockpick."

He leaves a beat, then asks the last question more quietly. "I won't open it. You have my word, and I keep that one. But I'd like to know what I'm carrying, at least from the outside. How big is it, how heavy, and is there a key? Does Thole have one, or did Aubrey keep it?"

Nobody touches the purse. Hesper looks at it, then at Bram, as though he had asked the right question first.

"The fifty is yours. It's yours whatever Thole asks." She opens the drawer again and lays a folded sheet beside the purse. It has been opened and closed so often it lies flat along its creases. "His notice. Read it."

It's written in a careful moneylender's hand that takes care over the figures. *To the widow of Master Aubrey Vallow.* One coffer of iron, banded, small enough for one man to carry, its hasp sealed in yellow wax, deposited by the said Master Vallow eight months since, against a loan of one hundred and twenty gold pieces. Redeemable until sundown of this day *by the bearer of the ticket, or the lawful heir producing it.* After that it falls forfeit to the undersigned. A buyer, Master Corwen Ashby, has declared his interest. *G. Thole, in his own hand.*

"A hundred and twenty," Hesper says. "If he'll take it lawfully, I'll pay it, and your hundred still stands. I can't go far past that." She answers Bram's other question in the same even tone. "I'm his widow and his heir. The will was proved before the temple court in the spring, and I hold the copy. I showed it to Thole the first time. He read it twice and said the terms stand as written. He wouldn't tell me whether that meant he'd take my money." A pause. "I have no ticket. There's no copy of the pledge in this house. I've been through his papers. It's the only paper I ever knew him not to keep."

She turns to you. "I never saw the coffer. What you've just read is all I know of it." She tips her chin at the rack of stamps and the dish of dull red wax. "Aubrey sealed in red. Every stamp in that rack is his, and every one takes red."

To Pell: "If there's a key, I haven't found it. The notice doesn't mention one."

Then back to Bram's last question. "I don't know what's in it. Nobody has warned me of anything. That notice is the only word anyone has sent me about it. Aubrey told me once, in this room: if it ever comes to you, keep it shut. He didn't say why, and I didn't ask." She answers that one faster than the others, and her eyes stay on the wax dish while she does.

The watcher next. "He's there when I open the upstairs shutters, before the bell. By the time I sit down to eat at noon, he's gone. It's been the same three days running. I don't know where he goes." She looks at Pell. "From upstairs I can see the corner, the trough, the cooper's step and a hat. I couldn't tell you which of them it is, or whether it's the same one every morning." To you, flatly: "He was courteous the first time. The second time he was in. I saw his lamp."

At Pell's promise she holds his eyes a moment longer than she has held anyone's. "I'll hold you to that."

When he looks at the shelves, she hesitates. Then she takes down two narrow books bound in calf, this year's and last year's, and sets them on the desk. "The day-books. Not the registers. Those are his clients' business, not mine to open."

Pell sits down at the dead man's desk and starts turning pages. He reads a long while, back through the year and into the one before, and at last his finger comes to rest on a page.

Hesper looks where his finger rests. "Sister Maudra Kell keeps the temple archive. Aubrey did the temple's leases and bequests for years. I saw those entries." Her eyes move to the margin and stay there. "That mark I don't know. It isn't one of his."

The bell of the Song of the Morning hasn't rung again. Half an hour has gone by since you came in off the lane, and the purse still sits on the desk where she put it.

Where you are: Aubrey Vallow's study, Hesper's house · Time: Day 1 · morning

The big man in mail steps up beside the desk. "What have you found, Pell?" He looks at the entry and the mark without touching the pages.

"Mistress Vallow, we'll try the lawful road first. We'll need that notice, your proved copy of the will, and your written authority to act for you. Keep the redemption money ready until we know whether Thole will accept it without the ticket."

Bram glances at you and Pell. "If he won't, we find out precisely why. Sister Maudra may be able to help us after that." Then he turns back to Hesper. "One other thing. Did Aubrey seem hurt or frightened when he told you to keep it shut? And was anyone with him when he fell?"

Pell takes Aubrey's pen from its rest. It's dry, so he dips it once in the inkwell and copies the mark onto a scrap of paper: the circle, the upright stroke, the little hook at the foot. His hand is steady. He blows the ink dry and tucks the scrap inside his coat. Then he finally reaches over and takes the purse, weighs it once in his palm, and sets it down nearer the middle of the desk.

"We'll take it." He turns the notice so you can both see one line, and taps it. "*By the bearer of the ticket, or the lawful heir producing it.* That's a moneylender's way of saying the ticket comes first. Aubrey kept every paper he ever touched except this one. So either he hid it, or he gave it to someone. If it's in a stranger's hand by sundown, Thole can hand the coffer over and call it lawful, and your will won't stop him. I'd wager Master Ashby knows where that ticket is, even if we don't."

He looks at Bram and you. "Here's how I'd cut it. Mistress Vallow goes to Thole with the hundred and twenty and the will, and she doesn't go alone. One of you walks in beside her. He shut his door on a widow. He won't do that to a man in chain mail with a writ in her hand, not in daylight on the main street. If he takes the money, we're done by noon." A pause. "If he won't, I want to know why. And I want to know where Thole keeps things, and whether Ashby has already been in to see it."

He nods toward the front of the house. "Our watcher leaves before noon. I'd like to see where he goes. I'll slip out the back over the yard wall and pick him up from the corner. The tiefling first, since he's the one who flinched." He holds up the folded scrap. "Then the temple. Sister Kell saw Aubrey twice in her archive, and this mark sits beside the second visit. If it's a temple sign, she'll know it. If it isn't, her face will tell me."

To Hesper, more quietly: "Is the yard gate barred, and does it come out on another lane? I'd rather nobody sees four of us leave by your front door."

The day-book lies open where Pell left it, and the entry is easy to read: *Song. Archive. Sr. M.K.* Beside it in the margin is the small inked figure, a circle with one upright stroke through it, hooked at the foot.

You lean in over the page, close enough to see the strokes of the ink. Your eyes have read every script ever put in front of them. They find nothing to read here: no letter, no glyph, no cipher. It is a drawing of something. The hand that made it went slowly and carefully, the way you copy a thing you have only seen once.

Hesper takes the questions in order, the way she takes everything.

"The notice is yours." She slides the folded sheet across to Bram. "The authority I'll write now." She sits for the first time since you came in, takes a clean sheet from the drawer and writes without stopping. She doesn't reach for the rack of stamps. "Those are his. I won't put his seal on my business." She signs it, sands it and hands it to Bram. It runs four lines: *I, Hesper Vallow, widow and proved heir of Aubrey Vallow, notary of Beregost, authorise the bearer, Bram Halloway, to treat on my behalf with Master Gaspar Thole for the redemption of the coffer named in his notice.* "The will doesn't leave this house unless I go with it. The money will be ready."

Then she answers Bram's last two questions. She rests her inked hand flat on the desk.

"He was tired. He had been tired since the autumn." That's all she says to the first one, and she lets it stand. "Nobody was with him. He went out before light, to the dawn service. He often did. A novice found him at the foot of the steps when she came to sweep. The temple's healer laid him out. She wrote that he fell."

To what you said about a lost ticket, Hesper shakes her head once. "It doesn't say the ticket is lost. It doesn't say where the ticket is at all. That's my word, not his." She turns the day-book a little toward you. "And the mark isn't beside Thole. He wrote *G.T.* and the hour, and nothing else. The mark is beside the temple." She pauses. "Sister Kell keeps the archive, not the court. Ask her whatever you like. But whatever she writes down goes into the temple's books."

She watches Pell set the purse in the middle of the desk. "Then it's agreed. The fifty is yours to divide as you see fit." She leaves it lying where he put it.

To the idea of walking into Thole's with one of you beside her: "I'll go. He has seen me twice. He hasn't seen me with company." Something in her face goes harder. "I would like to see him not open the door to a man in mail."

Last, the yard. "There's a door in the back wall, under the pear tree. It's bolted on this side and hasn't been opened since the winter. It gives onto the cart alley behind the smithies. The alley runs up behind the cooper's yard and comes out on the main street two doors below the trough." She stands. "I can be ready to go to Thole in a quarter of an hour. Tell me which of you is coming, and whether we go now or wait until your watcher has gone."

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: The coffer stays shut

Where you are: Aubrey Vallow's study, at the desk · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram tells Hesper, "I'll walk with you, Mistress Vallow. Bring the will and the redemption money. We go when you're ready—no sense letting the morning slip." He folds the authority and the notice carefully into his pack.

He turns to Pell. "Pell, we'll give you those fifteen minutes to get into place. I won't hail you if I spot you. Mind yourself; we don't yet know that either fellow is watching this house."

To you he says, "I'd welcome you beside us at Thole's. Another pair of ears may be worth more than the mail." Then he loosens his sword belt a notch so the hilt sits comfortably, leaving the blade sheathed. "We're going to offer payment, not threaten him. Let him give us his answer plainly."

Pell takes the fifty and counts it out on the desk in three piles: seventeen, seventeen, sixteen. He leaves the two larger piles on the wood in front of Bram and you and pockets the smallest without comment. Hesper watches him do it and says nothing.

"Go now," he tells Hesper. "Don't wait for him to leave. I want him to see you walk down that lane with Bram beside you. If he's only watching the house, he'll stay put. If he's watching for the coffer, he'll run to whoever pays him the moment you turn toward Thole's. Either way, I'll learn something."

He looks at Bram. "Give me a count of a hundred before you open the front door. I'll be in the alley by then. Walk slowly, and don't look at the corner. Let him have a good look at you."

To you: "Your choice. Thole's with them, or the temple. If you go to Sister Kell, don't show her the mark first. Ask about Aubrey's visits and watch how she answers. Then show her." He touches something inside his coat. "I'll keep my copy, so we've each got one if you want to draw your own. Whatever she writes down goes in their books, so tell her as little as you can."

He looks around at all three of you. "Thole's front step, or the cooper's corner, at noon. Whoever isn't there by the bell, the rest go looking." Then he goes out to the yard.

Hesper listens to Bram with her eyes on the folded papers as they go into his pack. "Give me a quarter of an hour. The will is upstairs, and so is the money." She says nothing about the sword belt. Her eyes drop to it once and come back up.

She answers your question at once. "No. Not drawn, not cut, not anywhere. I would remember." She looks at the day-book a moment longer. "And Ashby isn't in either book. I looked for him the day the notice came." When you suggest the alley, she shakes her head once. "I've gone out by that front door every day for twenty-two years. I'm not leaving my own house by the cart alley to go and pay a debt." Then, a little less flatly, to you: "Come with me. I'd be glad of it."

She goes up the stairs, and you hear a floorboard and a drawer overhead.

After a while the floorboard creaks again, and Hesper comes down. She has a dark cloak over the grey coat. She carries a leather document case under one arm and a drawstring purse in her hand, and she holds the purse the way people hold money they can't spare. "The will, the proving, and a hundred and twenty," she says. "Counted twice." She goes down the hall to the front door and puts her hand on the bar, but she doesn't lift it. It's a little past nine. She waits for Bram and you.

Where you are: Hesper's front hall, at the barred door · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram pockets his seventeen gold and joins Hesper at the door.

"Ready. You lead us to his shop; I'll stay beside you."

Hesper lifts the bar herself. She lays it against the wall, opens the door onto the bright lane and steps out without looking toward the corner. Bram comes out at her right shoulder, his seventeen gold in his purse, his hand nowhere near his sword. You take the far side, away from the trough, and turn your head down the lane as if you were waiting for the morning cart. Behind you the study is empty. Your seventeen gold lies on the dead man's desk where you left it.

You walk up the lane at Hesper's pace, which is quick and even. Bram keeps an easy stride, watching the doorways and the people ahead. The coal cart has finished at the smithy yard. Hammers ring on both sides of you.

The tiefling in the cooper's doorway sees a man in mail coming and steps down off the step to make room. He ducks his head the way people do when they're used to being looked at. He doesn't watch you pass.

The stable lad does watch you, the way anyone watches a man in mail. Then his eyes go back to the carts. He sits on the trough with no horse, no bucket and no fork.

It's no bigger than a psalter. She doesn't open it at once. She sets it on the table beside the chained rolls and keeps her palm on the cover.

"You asked me plainly, Master Halloway, so I'll answer you the same way. Yes. He asked me about a seal." She opens the book. "This house made four of them, two hundred years ago, for the dawn office. There are four drawings on the open page, done in brown ink by a careful hand much older than Aubrey's. Each one is a circle split by an upright key, the same figure as Bram's scrap. They aren't all the same, though. Each key has a different foot: a plain bar on the first, a split on the second, a ring on the third. The fourth ends in a small hook. A line of tiny letters runs round each rim. Under all four, in a different and later ink, someone has written a single entry: *Lost, all four, in the fire of the chapter house. Year of the Bright Blade.* That was ninety years ago.

You can't help reading the rim script, any more than you can help reading a shop sign. It's an old, formal dawn-script, and it says the same thing around each of the four: *Witnessed at the light. It answers the hand it was given.*

"The hook," Maudra says. "That's the fourth. Aubrey drew it from the thing itself, not from this page. I showed him this page afterwards, and he went white." She closes the book. "The register says it burned. So either the register is wrong, or someone took it out of this house before the fire and kept quiet about it for ninety years."

She doesn't sit down.

"He asked me how one is opened. I'll tell you what I told him. It isn't broken. It's opened, by the hand it was set for. Any other hand, and what lies under it is gone. Burnt to nothing inside the box, and the box still shut." Her voice stays brisk, but it's quieter now. "Whose hand that one was set for, he didn't tell me. I didn't ask. I thought there would be time."

She looks at Bram, then at you, and this time she holds your eyes.

"So now I owe two things. One is to a dead man, who left me something for his widow. The other is to this house, which has a seal sitting on a moneylender's shelf that by its own register burned before I was born." She lays her hand flat on the saffron boards. "I mean to keep both, if I can."

"Bring me her two lines, and I'll do what he asked of me. But when that coffer comes out of Thole's, I'll want to see that wax with my own eyes before anyone carries it further. Here, or on her own step. I don't mind which." A pause. "Will she allow that? Or must I go to Brother Lucan instead and tell him what's sitting at Thole's?"

Below the high windows the cloister is quiet. Somewhere in the garden the bean-row brother is humming.

Where you are: At Sister Maudra's archive door, top of the chapter house stair · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram turns to Sister Maudra. "Come with us now, if you're able, Sister. We'll wait for Lucan, then go to Thole's and straight to Hesper's step. Better than leaving you uncertain when to come."

He looks to you and the ticket. "That stays safe with you. We have what we need to redeem it."

To Maudra he adds, "Our missing companion is Pell Dunmore. If he comes asking after us, please have word left that we're taking the lawful route through Lucan and Thole, then back to Hesper."

You read the stiff little card twice in the stair light, fold it back into Aubrey's paper along his creases and put it in an inner pocket. Sister Maudra watches it go in and doesn't comment.

She answers Bram first.

"Come down with you now. To Lucan's table, then a moneylender's counter, then the main street." She repeats it back to him like a list of shelf-marks, and her tone makes it plain what she thinks of the list. "A sister of this house walking into Gaspar Thole's behind a man in mail. By the evening office every forge in Beregost would have it that the temple had come to take a widow's box away from her. No, Master Halloway."

Then you offer her the yard door under the pear tree, and the old woman goes quiet for a moment.

"Her step, she said." Maudra considers it. "Her back step is as much hers as her front one, and nobody sits on a trough to watch it." She gives a short nod. "The yard, then. When it's out of Thole's and on its way to her, send Brother Teo up my stair. I'll come round by the garden and the forge boys' path. I walked it when I was young enough to be scolded for it." She doesn't say how long ago that was. "I'll be slower than you. Don't take it inside before I get there."

She hears the last thing you say, about keeping both debts, all of it, and for a moment she just looks at you.

"See that you do, Mistress."

On Pell she doesn't need telling twice. "Dunmore. If anyone comes asking under that name, Teo will tell him you've gone to Lucan and then to Thole's, and then to the widow." She puts her hand on the door. "Go on. You've less afternoon than you think."

The iron-bound door shuts behind you before you reach the second step.

Brother Teo is at the bottom of the stair. Bram asks him for the next available hearing: "We've found the ticket. The warden asked to see it before the lender does. We'll wait our turn." Teo follows you back along the east walk without being asked. The antechamber is cool and dim. The wheelwright's voice is still rising and falling behind the inner door, something about a hub and whether a spoke counts as a fault if it only cracked once it was on the road. Teo sits down at his table, finds Bram's line in the book and writes a second one under it in his small upright hand: *Bram Halloway, again. The ticket.* He sands it and adds Maudra's message for Pell in the margin below.

"After the wheelwright," he says. "He's nearly done. He's started saying the same things twice."

He turns out to be right. You wait a little under half an hour on the bench. The slab of light from the high window creeps across the floor, and nobody comes in from the square. Then the inner door opens, and a big man with sawdust in his beard comes out, still arguing over his shoulder. Brother Lucan stands in the doorway behind him. He sees you and Bram on the bench and lifts his eyebrows a fraction.

"That was quick," he says. "Come in."

He sits down at the long table and holds out his hand, as he did this morning. You take Aubrey's folded paper from your pocket and open it on the table yourself. You don't let go of the card until his fingers are on it.

Lucan reads the outside first, *For my widow, if it comes to it. A.V.*, and says the initials quietly to the page. Then he reads the ticket, once quickly and once slowly with a finger under the lines. The finger stops on *the hasp sealed in yellow* and stays there a moment longer than the words need. He says nothing about it. He moves on to *No. 41. G. Thole*, takes down a red-bound book from the shelf behind him, finds a page and runs his finger down a column.

"Thole registers his ticket numbers with this court every quarter, so nobody can forge them. Forty-one, issued in the month Aubrey's day-book gives." He closes the book and squares the card in front of him with two fingers. "It's real."

He leans back.

"You understand what you're holding? *By the bearer of my ticket.* Mistress Marrin is the bearer, sent by the heir. Thole's own terms require him to take a hundred and twenty from her across his counter, and he doesn't need a word from me to do it." He taps Thole's undertaking, which Bram has laid beside the ticket. "He asked for my seal because he had no ticket in front of him. Now there is one."

"Even so, I'll write it if you want it. A ruling that the heir's redemption, made by her bearer with this ticket, ends every other claim on the coffer, Master Ashby's included, from the moment the money is paid. Thole can show it to anyone who comes knocking afterwards, and so can she." He folds his ink-stained hands on the table. "Two gold. It goes in the book under the pledge, with you as applicant, Master Halloway. Do you want it, or will you take the ticket to Thole as it is?"

Through the window behind him the bean-row brother has started on the far poles. It's getting on for twenty to two.

*(Out of game: no rolls this round. Maudra made her own choice, and Lucan checked the ticket against the court's own register.)*

Where you are: Brother Lucan's hearing room, temple · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram says, "Yes, please. With Ashby's claim expressly covered, as you said."

He sets two gold pieces on the table.

"Enter me as applicant under Aubrey's pledge, as we agreed. We'd also be grateful for a receipt for the fee."

Then he asks the warden, "If Thole refuses the ticket and payment despite this ruling, whom should we fetch?"

Brother Lucan looks at the two gold pieces on the table and leaves them where Bram put them while he hears the rest.

"Applicant, Bram Halloway. Under the pledge of A. Vallow, deceased, to G. Thole." He takes a sheet from the drawer, a heavier stock than the petition book's, and uncaps his ink. "A receipt as well. You'll have both."

He writes slowly in a small, upright court hand and doesn't stop to think. You make your case for the seal while he writes. He doesn't look up, but at *argue with the temple instead of with Hesper* the pen pauses for half a word and then goes on. When he's done, he turns the sheet round on the table for you both to read:

*Court of contracts of the Song of the Morning. On the application of Bram Halloway, under the pledge of A. Vallow, deceased, to G. Thole, lender on surety. The court has seen ticket No. 41 in the lender's hand, entered in this court's register of his tickets. It rules: redemption of the coffer named therein, made before sundown of the term by the bearer of that ticket, sent by the lawful heir and proved here in the spring, ends the pledge and every other claim on the coffer from the moment the sum is paid, including any claim of purchase by Master Corwen Ashby or any other. L. Pryce, warden.*

He sands it and takes a small box down from the shelf behind him. It's plain wood, and inside is a brass seal with a rayed sun. He warms a stick of saffron wax at the candle, lets a coin-sized pool fall at the foot of the sheet, and presses the sun into it. He holds it there for a breath, then lifts it. The rays come up clean.

The receipt takes him less time: *Received of Bram Halloway, two gold pieces, the court's fee for a ruling under the pledge of A. Vallow. L. Pryce.* He sweeps the two coins into a drawer and slides the receipt across after the ruling. Then he picks up ticket No. 41, folds it back into Aubrey's paper along its old creases, and gives it to you rather than Bram.

"The bearer carries the ticket," he says. "Keep it that way until it's on Thole's counter."

Then he gets to Bram's last question. He puts his hand flat on the court book while he answers.

"If Gaspar Thole sees that seal and still won't take a lawful redemption, come back to this room before the bell. I'll send Brother Teo to his door with a summons, and he'll stand in that chair and explain himself to me. A lender in Beregost who defies this court's seal lends to nobody for long, and he knows it." He takes his hand off the book. "He won't refuse. He asked for this. What he'll do is read it twice, wipe his palms, and look at his door."

He squares the court book on the shelf with two fingers and sits back.

"I'll want to hear when it's done, Master Halloway. Before the square does."

The sheet with the court's sun on it lies on the table in front of Bram, still warm at the foot. Outside the window the bean-row brother has worked his way down to the far poles. It's a little before two o'clock. Hesper's door is the length of the main street away, and Thole's is on the way there.

Where you are: the warden's court of contracts room, Song of the Morning temple, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram speaks to Brother Lucan: "You'll hear from us when it's done. Thank you, Brother."

Brother Lucan watches Bram leave the ruling flat on the table until the saffron wax has gone from glossy to dull. Only then does Bram slide it into his pack between the undertaking and the notice, where the stiff sheets on either side will keep it from bending. The receipt goes in after it.

You put Aubrey's folded paper back in your inner pocket and press it flat with your palm. When you say you'd rather carry the news yourself than leave it to a carter, the warden looks up at you.

"So would I, Mistress." He's already reaching for the next blank sheet. "A carter tells it wrong, and then I have to hear it twice."

That's the end of it. He doesn't get up. The inner door swings half shut behind you.

You're halfway across the antechamber when Brother Teo looks up from his pens. He was waiting for you, and he puts a finger on his book before Bram reaches the propped door.

"Master Halloway. There's word for you." He turns the book around. Under Bram's two lines, in the same small upright hand, is a third: *Pell Dunmore, for Master Halloway.* Below it Teo has written the message. "He came in while you were with the warden, a quarter of an hour ago, maybe a little less. Lean, quick, grit on his knees. I told him you were inside. I don't interrupt the warden, so he left this." Teo reads it out exactly, the way a clerk does: "*That I'm here, and that I'll meet them at the garden wicket on the east lane, not out front. He'll know why.*" He looks up. "He said something about a cart to catch as well. Then he went out by the square door and turned left along the wall."

Maudra's message for Pell is still in the margin next to it, written before he ever arrived.

Through the propped door the square is bright and nearly empty in the early afternoon. The great steps rise on the right. Past them, down the main street and too far off to see a face, is the alehouse bench. Left along the chapter house wall, in its strip of shade, is the buttress at the corner and the east lane behind it, where you and Bram came out of the footway an hour ago. From the wicket that footway runs behind the houses all the way to the cooper's yard and the cart alley.

It's a little before two.

Where you are: chapter house antechamber, by Teo's desk near the propped square door · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Bram says to Brother Teo, "Good. Thank you for keeping his words straight."

He turns to you. "Let's hear him before we walk out front. He may know who that bench is watching."

Brother Teo nods at the thanks as if it were part of the job, and maybe it is. He's already sanding a line in his book before Bram turns away.

You let Bram step out first and follow two paces behind him, keeping to the shade.

The square is bright and quiet in the early afternoon. Water runs in the fountain with nobody at it. Bram turns left at once and keeps close to the chapter house wall, where the temple's shadow runs in a strip about an arm wide. He walks at the pace of a man with an errand but no hurry. You come behind him at the same pace, one hand loose at your side, looking like a woman who happens to be going the same way.

The great steps rise on your right. For a few strides before the steps cut it off, the main street opens up between the last roofs, all the way down to the alehouse hatch. The big man is still on the end of the bench with his legs out across the cobbles and a cup at his elbow, too far off to see his face. His head is turned toward the foot of the steps and the square in front of them. It isn't turned toward the strip of shade along the wall. Then the steps come between you and him, and there's only rose granite on your right and whitewash on your left.

Nobody calls out, and no one in the square looks your way twice.

At the buttress on the corner the wall turns, and you step out of the square into the east lane. The sheds are on one side. On the other is the long garden wall with its plank wicket and the latch-string hanging through its hole. Across the lane, between the two woodstores, is the narrow mouth of the footway you and Bram came out of an hour ago. Over the wall the bean poles stand in their pairs, and a brother in a straw hat is bent over the far rows with his back to the cloister. It's a few minutes past two.

*(Out of game: under the retcon we agreed, Pell is waiting by this wicket at about 14:03, so your threads meet here. Bram's words to him will be heard when his player answers next round, in the joined scene.)*

Where you are: east lane, by the garden wicket · Time: Day 1 · evening

Bram rounds the buttress ahead of you. Pell comes off the garden wall as he does and meets you both halfway down the lane, so the three of you stop in the shed's shadow with the corner of the temple between you and the square. The plank wicket is a few steps behind him. Across the ruts is the gap between the two woodstores. From down here it's only a dark slot between stacked logs. Up close you can see coal grit on Pell's knees and tar on his coat.

Bram stops where he leaves the lane clear and keeps his voice under the hum of the bees.

"We looked for you at noon. Glad you're on your feet. We've got Aubrey's ticket and the court's sealed ruling. Hesper has the redemption money ready at home."

He glances back toward the corner, then turns to Pell. "What did you find—and what's this cart we need to catch?"

Pell keeps his voice low and gives it to you short.

"Don't go back out front. Ashby's big sunburnt man is on the alehouse bench across from Thole's with a cup. He can see Thole's door, the street both ways and the foot of the great steps. He's been there since noon and he doesn't care who sees him." He glances past Bram's shoulder toward the corner. "Did you come round the front of the steps just now, or along the chapter house wall?"

He doesn't wait long for the answer.

"Short version of my morning. The watcher's a stable lad at the Red Sheaf, north end. A man in a grey riding cloak pays him silver at the noon bell to tell what he saw. The lad told him three of you went out, a shield and two women, and which way you turned. The chandler across the street has the man on his slate in his own hand as *Ashby & Corve*, an iron buyer, there near a tenday. He has two hired swords. The big one's on that bench. A thin one rides out before light and comes back after dark." A beat. "And yesterday Ashby bought two flasks of good lamp oil and a new tinderbox. I don't like that, with a sealed box he's meant to be buying."

He nods back toward the chapter house.

"Hesper told me Thole's terms: no money without a ticket, unless the court of contracts gives him a sealed writing that the heir's redemption ends it. Teo told me the warden sent you up to Sister Maudra before noon, and that's all I know." He looks from Bram to you. "So. Does the court give the writing? What did the archivist want with you? And how long have we got before the warden stops hearing?"

He tips his head at the gap between the woodstores across the lane.

"That path runs west behind the houses, toward the cooper's end. I haven't walked it yet. If we're carrying anything out of Thole's later, I'd rather bring it back that way than past the bench."

He doesn't say a word about the cart.

Over the wall the old brother in the straw hat has straightened up between two bean poles. He watches the three of you muttering beside his gate the way a man watches weather coming. Nobody looks back at him. After a moment he sniffs, bends again and goes on pinching blackfly into his clay pot.

Nobody else is in the lane. The cat on the shed roofs has its eyes shut. From the square round the corner comes the sound of the fountain, and nothing else. It's a few minutes past two, and Pell is waiting for answers.

*(Out of game: this was honest talk, so no roll. You told Pell that you carry the ticket, that Maudra found it and that Bram has the court's seal. You asked him about the cart rather than telling him about it, and he left that unanswered.)*

Bram stands beside Hesper, his hands well clear of his sword. "Then let's keep to the writing," he says evenly. "May we see the rest of that entry, beneath your thumb?" He goes on: "You're right that a missing ticket leaves a claim unsettled. But how does three hundred gold settle it where a hundred and twenty won't? Would you give her a written release against any later bearer?" He pauses. "And is there a lawful way to cancel the missing ticket before sundown—a declaration before the temple court, or a surety? We'd rather pay for that than buy the same coffer twice."

Thole hears Bram out without moving his thumb. When Bram asks to see the rest of the entry, he looks down at his own hand as if he'd forgotten it was there.

"That line is my own note, Master Halloway. It isn't one of his terms." He closes the ledger gently, the way you close a book on a sleeping cat, and keeps his palm on the cover. "The terms are all above it, and you've read them."

He takes the other questions in order, like items on a bill.

"A release from the mistress binds the mistress. It doesn't bind a stranger with a ticket in his hand. He'd come to me, not to her." He spreads his soft fingers. "Three hundred doesn't settle his claim. It pays for it. If he comes, I pay him out of the difference and I'm no worse off. That's what surety means."

"A declaration of loss, yes, that can be done. The court of contracts sits at the Song. You swear the ticket lost, the court posts notice on the temple door, and anyone holding it has a tenday to come forward." He gives Hesper a small, regretful look. "A tenday, mistress. Your term ends tonight."

Then you speak. At *the court would say so* his eyes go to your face, then to the green door behind him, then to the bolted street door. He wipes his palms down the front of his brown coat. You are watching for it, and from where you stand you see what Bram can't from the side: the mention of a court doesn't frighten him. It interests him. Something in his face eases a little, like a man hearing a door he thought was locked turn out to be only shut.

You press the point gently, as if explaining it to a patient's family.

Got it. Sefa's speech goes into the turn as written: the pause, the argument that a redeemed pledge leaves a later ticket-holder with a quarrel against the Vallow estate and not against Thole, and the closing line about the hundred and twenty on the counter. Her reading of the clause is her own argument made aloud. Whether Thole accepts it is still for the die to settle.

One detail doesn't match what's been established. The ledger isn't closed. Thole turned it round to face you and it's lying open on the counter, with his finger on the entry. I'll have Sefa nod at the open ledger instead. Nothing else changes.

The card stands as called: Persuasion, DC 15, with her +7, at advantage. Her speech is the kind of case that card was called for, so it doesn't add anything beyond what's already on it. Roll when you're ready, and I'll play Thole's answer from what the die decides.

screens.text:
The session begins.

Beregost is already at work. Hammers ring from the smithies down the lane, a cart rattles past toward the Trade Way, and the last note of Lathander's morning bell fades over the rooftops.

The oak door opens a hand's width, then wider. Hesper Vallow stands in the gap. She is a spare woman in a plain grey coat, ink on two fingers of her right hand. She looks at each of you in turn: Bram with his painted-over shield, Sefa, and you. Then her gaze goes past you, up the lane toward the main street, and stays there a moment too long.

"All three of you. Good." Behind her the hall is dim. Every shutter on the ground floor is closed against the sun. "By nightfall, as I said. Not an hour later." She steps back from the threshold and holds the door, but she doesn't explain yet. She is waiting to see who comes in first, or whether anyone has something to ask her out here on the step.

Your records:
Pell Dunmore — Human, rogue 5 (Thief), Lower City roof-runner turned hireling, level 5
HP 33/33 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet
STR 10 · DEX 17 · CON 13 · INT 13 · WIS 12 · CHA 12
Skills: Stealth +9 (expertise); Sleight of Hand +6; Acrobatics +6; Perception +4; Investigation +4; Insight +4; Tools: thieves' tools +9 (expertise)
Saves: Dexterity saving throw +6 (proficient); Intelligence saving throw +4 (proficient); Strength saving throw +0; Constitution saving throw +1; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +1
Attacks: Shortsword +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing; Dagger +6 to hit, 1d4+3 piercing, thrown 20/60; Shortbow +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 80/320; Sneak Attack: +3d6 once a turn with advantage or an ally beside the target
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Sneak Attack 3d6; Cunning Action: Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action; Uncanny Dodge: a reaction halves the damage of an attack he can see; Fast Hands (Thief): a bonus action to use an object — a potion on another, a lock, a lamp; Second-Story Work: climbs at full speed; Thieves' Cant
Limits: Light armour; 33 hit points — he cannot stand at the front for long; Sneak Attack needs advantage or an ally beside the target
Counters: Hit dice 5/5
Money: 31 gp; 2 ep; 6 sp; 55 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Thieves' Tools; Main hand: Shortsword
Pack: Arrow ×20; Bedroll and Rations; Dagger ×2; Flask of Oil ×2; Hooded Lantern; Potion of Healing ×3; Shortbow; Silk Rope (50 feet)

Where you are: on the step outside Hesper Vallow's oak door, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram glances up the lane where Hesper was looking, and your eyes follow his a moment later. Sefa gives Hesper a small nod. "Nightfall, then," she says quietly. "We'll hear it inside, I think. Better than on the step." Bram goes in, sword sheathed. "Best talk away from the street, then. What needs doing by nightfall—and who are you watching for?"

It's an ordinary Beregost morning. A coal cart is backing into the smithy yard at the bottom of the lane. At the top, where the lane meets the main street, a horse trough stands by the corner. A stable lad sits on its edge with straw on his sleeves, picking at a heel of bread and watching the carts. Across from him, in the shade of the cooper's doorway, a tiefling in a road-dusty coat leans on the wall. When your look reaches him, he turns away quickly, toward the cooper's shut door, and finds something to study in the planking. The lad doesn't turn at all. He just keeps eating.

Bram goes in first and steps to the left of the doorway. Sefa comes right behind him with her small, unhurried nod. You come last, out of the sun, and stop where you can still see a hand's width of the lane through the gap.

The hall smells of beeswax and cold ashes. Hesper shuts the door, drops the bar, and stands a moment with her palm flat on the oak.

"Someone has stood at the top of the lane three mornings running," she says. "Young, I think. I see him from the upstairs window, and never well. I don't know who he is. I don't know who sends him." She looks at you. "You're right about the street. Come through."

She takes you down the hall, past a front room where the furniture sits under dust sheets, to a study at the back. Its one window looks onto a walled yard with a rain barrel and a pear tree. Shelves of bound ledgers cover two walls. A notary's desk sits under the window, tidy and unused, with a rack of seal-stamps and a dish of red wax that has gone dull with dust. Hesper doesn't sit. She stands behind the desk, her inked hand resting on its edge.

"My husband was Aubrey Vallow, notary of this town for twenty years. He died this winter. He fell on the steps of the Song of the Morning." She says it like an entry in a register. "Eight months ago he pledged an iron coffer to a moneylender on the main street, Gaspar Thole. I didn't know until last week, when Thole sent me a courtesy notice as the widow. The term of the pledge ends at sundown today. After that, Thole may sell it, and he has a buyer. A Master Corwen Ashby. I don't know him."

"I have been to Thole twice. The first time he was polite and told me nothing. The second time he didn't open the door."

From a drawer she takes a leather purse and sets it on the desk. It's heavy, and it stays where she put it.

"The terms. I want the coffer brought here, to this room, before sundown. Fifty gold now, a hundred more on delivery. How you get it from Thole is your affair, provided nothing is done that puts my name before the temple court. And one condition, which isn't negotiable." She raises her eyes to each of you in turn. "It comes to me shut. Not opened, not tried, not looked into. Aubrey asked me to keep it shut, and I mean to."

She waits with her hand beside the purse and doesn't push it toward any of you.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Aubrey Vallow's coffer
+ Quest: Aubrey Vallow's coffer

Where you are: Hesper's back study · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram leaves the purse where it is. "Is that fifty our advance, or the money to redeem the pledge? How much does Thole say he's owed—and have you papers showing your right to collect it?" He glances at the dusty seal-stamps, then back to her. "I can agree to leave it shut. But before we take your coin: what do you know of what's inside, and has anyone besides your husband warned you against opening it? If there's danger in carrying it, we need to know."

Sefa folds her hands in front of her and makes no move toward the purse. "We'll take it on. But before that purse changes hands, tell us three things plainly," she says, her voice low and even. "Do you have Aubrey's note of pledge—the number of the debt, the surety written? If we walk into Thole's shop with nothing but a widow's word, he can name any sum and shut the door again." She glances at the closed window and back to Hesper. "And the coffer itself. You said iron. Is it small enough to carry under one arm, or will we need a cart and two strong backs? Has it any mark we can swear to—a scratch, a lockplate, a letter, a way of proving it is your husband's and not some other man's coffer?" A pause. "And the watcher at the top of the lane. These three mornings—when does he stop? Does he stay after the doors open, or only until someone shows at a window? Thole may not have been as courteous as his notice."

Nobody touches the purse. Hesper looks at it, then at Bram, as though he had asked the right question first.

"The fifty is yours. It's yours whatever Thole asks." She opens the drawer again and lays a folded sheet beside the purse. It has been opened and closed so often it lies flat along its creases. "His notice. Read it."

It's written in a careful moneylender's hand that takes care over the figures. *To the widow of Master Aubrey Vallow.* One coffer of iron, banded, small enough for one man to carry, its hasp sealed in yellow wax, deposited by the said Master Vallow eight months since, against a loan of one hundred and twenty gold pieces. Redeemable until sundown of this day *by the bearer of the ticket, or the lawful heir producing it.* After that it falls forfeit to the undersigned. A buyer, Master Corwen Ashby, has declared his interest. *G. Thole, in his own hand.*

"A hundred and twenty," Hesper says. "If he'll take it lawfully, I'll pay it, and your hundred still stands. I can't go far past that." She answers Bram's other question in the same even tone. After a few minutes the lane narrows between two yard walls and comes out into the cart alley behind the smithies. It's rutted and black with coal grit, the same as it was this morning. The footway runs on toward the temple end along the backs of the main-street houses, too narrow for a cart. You don't go down it. You stop at its mouth as if to retie a lace and count the back walls by their chimneys.

The fifth wall past the cooper's stands higher than its neighbours: close to ten feet of grey stone with fresh limewash. Broken crockery is set in mortar along the top, the way careful men in the Lower City top their walls. In the wall there's a single narrow door, iron-studded and flush with the stone, with no handle on this side that you can see. Above it, on the upper floor, is one shuttered window. Low down near the foot of the wall, just above the dirt of the footway, is a small square vent. It's barred with three iron rods and black inside. Nothing about it says what room it breathes for. All the other houses along that row have kitchen doors and slop-drains, and this one has neither.

You finish with the lace and walk the last few yards up the alley to the cooper's yard gate. Past the corner of the cooper's house you can see the main street. The trough at the top of Hesper's lane stands empty. Nobody's sitting on its rim now, and there's only a wet ring on the stone where someone set a bucket down. Down the lane Hesper's door is shut and her shutters are closed. It's a little past a quarter after one.

"If it's in this house at all, it's in the registers. Those are his clients' business. I told you so this morning." She leaves it at that and doesn't offer to open them.

The cart alley is as it was. The bellows boy is on his handle and the coal grit is warm underfoot. You don't go out to the main street this time. The hammers drop behind you as the smithies give way to gardens.

The Song of the Morning comes up over the rooftops: rose granite, the tower catching the full afternoon sun. Its back is a long garden wall with a wicket gate in it. Over the wall you can see a brother in a straw hat bent over the bean rows, and beyond the garden a row of small high windows along the chapter house. You follow the wall round the temple's east flank, where the chapter house stands between you and the square. In this lane the only thing that can see you is the tower.

Beyond it the great steps go up to the gold doors. A novice is sweeping the top of the steps. Drovers are watering a pair of mules at the fountain.

The sunburnt man is still on the end of the bench, his legs stretched across the cobbles and a fresh cup at his elbow. From there he has a clear view of the foot of the steps. The forty feet of wall from the buttress to the chapter house door is almost all in the temple's shadow, and the steps stand between it and the bench.

The thin rider is nowhere in sight. Neither is anyone else you would know.

It's getting on for a quarter to two.

Where you are: inside the archive at the top of the stair, with Sister Maudra · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sister Maudra doesn't sit down. She hears you out on her feet with one hand on the back of the reading-table chair. When you get to the garden wicket she turns her head toward the propped window at the far end and looks at it.

"The beans." She says it as though she were writing down where something is shelved. "The garden door is the cellarer's. He leaves it on the latch until the evening office and bars it after." She looks back at you. "So that way is open until the bell, and after the bell it isn't."

The window stays propped a hand's width open. Bees go past it, and below it the old brother in the bean rows is still humming, the same few notes over and over. Nothing on the stair behind you creaks.

When you get to the man on the bench, the one who doesn't hide and lets Thole see him through the grille, Maudra's mouth goes thin.

"Then he isn't sitting there to watch anybody. He's sitting there to be seen." She turns that over. "A man sends a sword to sit across from a lender's door when he expects the lender to sell to him at sundown and wants him to remember it. Gaspar Thole would sell his own coat to a man who frightened him. He'd tell himself it was the terms."

She leaves Thole there and comes to your last question. She takes her time with it, and she doesn't hide that she's choosing what to say.

"A box or a fire." She repeats it flatly. "A box, Master Dunmore. It won't catch light on its own while you carry it. Carry it by the bands and keep everyone's thumbs off the wax. I've told Master Halloway the same." Her hands go still at her waist. "As for the oil, I can only tell you what I make of it. A man who buys oil for a thing he's paying good gold for doesn't care what's in it. He wants nobody else to read it. That tells you it's worth reading, and someone has worked out what it would cost them if it were read."

That's all she gives you. She doesn't say what it holds, and she says nothing of their errand or of anything else in her keeping. She goes down the long room to a shelf halfway along, takes down a thick roll-book, carries it back and opens it at the far end of the table from you. She starts reading with one finger under the lines, as if you were furniture she has agreed to keep in the room.

"When they come, I'll hear the bell-pull," she says without looking up. "So will you."

The light from the high windows lies slantwise across the table. The stair stays quiet and the bell-pull doesn't move. Through the propped window comes the brother's humming, the scrape of a hoe, and once, far off in the town, a cart. It's getting on for four o'clock.

You can wait here as long as you like. Nothing changes in the archive until someone pulls that bell.

Where you are: the archive's long reading room, on the bench by the door · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sister Maudra doesn't look up from her roll-book at first. Her finger finishes its line before she answers.

"The end window." She says it flatly, the way she'd note where a book had been moved to. "Stand back from it, and leave the prop where it is. If that shutter swings, the cellarer will be up my stair asking why." Then she goes back to her reading, and that's all the permission you get.

You walk the length of the long room on quiet feet. You go wide around the lectern and its chained black book, past shelves of rolls tied with faded tape. The floorboards hold still under you in a way they didn't under Bram's mail. You stop to one side of the propped window, a pace back from the light, where the sill's shadow covers you and the gap still gives you a view.

The angle is better than you expected. Straight below is the gravel path through the bean rows to the cellarer's low door. The old brother is still at the far poles with his straw hat tipped back, working down the last pair. Past the garden wall is the plank wicket with its string hanging, and past that the east lane: the rutted stretch where the shadow of the shed roofs now reaches almost to the wall, and the stacks of firewood the carter left. Across the lane, between two woodstores, there's a narrow gap you couldn't see properly from the ground. A footpath barely a shield wide comes out of it. You can follow it with your eye a little way west along the backs of the main-street houses before the roofs hide it. It runs the same way as the footway behind the cooper's, toward the town.

The lane stays quiet. A girl drives three geese along it with a stick and goes out the far end. The cat is back on the shed roofs, asleep now. Nobody stops at the wicket, and nobody comes out of the gap between the woodstores. The stair behind you and the bell-pull by the door stay silent. Behind you Maudra turns a page about once a minute.

From the window the tower's shadow lies long across the cloister roofs to the east. It's a little after four.

Where you are: end window of the abbey library · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sister Maudra finishes her line before she answers, the way she has every time you've spoken. Her finger stays on the page.

"An hour, near enough. A little under at midsummer." She turns the page. "The cellarer bars his door on his way into choir. The brothers eat after the office, not before. He's not been late to choir in all the years I've known him, and he's proud of it." She goes back to her reading. "You'll hear the bell from that window better than I do from this end."

You thank her and keep watching.

Down in the garden the old brother has reached the last pair of poles. He stands up, rubs the small of his back with both fists, tips the clay pot over the compost heap by the wall and knocks it out on his palm. Then he picks up his hoe and walks back up the gravel path toward the cellarer's door, still humming. The door opens and shuts behind him. Now the bean rows are empty, and the poles throw long stripes of shadow across the gravel.

A few minutes later something moves in the gap between the woodstores. A boy comes out of the footpath into the east lane. He's lanky, in a leather apron burnt through in a dozen places, and he carries an empty wicker basket on one hip. He doesn't look round or hurry, and he doesn't glance at the wicket. He crosses to the sheds where the carter stacked the firewood, loads the basket with split logs until it's heaped, gets it up onto his shoulder and goes back into the gap the way he came. The footpath takes him and the roofs hide him a few yards in. From the window you can see that the path is used, and that a boy with a full basket fits in it without turning sideways.

After that the lane is empty again. The cat on the shed roofs has rolled into the last patch of sun. The shadow of the sheds now covers the ruts and climbs the foot of the garden wall. Nobody stops at the wicket. The bell-pull by the archive door stays still, and nothing comes up the stair.

It's about twenty past four. Nothing else happens at this window before the bell unless you want it to.

Where you are: at the archive window overlooking the garden and east lane · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Sister Maudra finishes her line before she looks up.

"Walk the path, look at the wall, come back inside half an hour." She says it back to you flatly, the way she'd read a catalogue entry. "If they pull my bell, I'll tell them what you said. Whether they wait is up to them." Then she goes back to her page.

You go down the long room, keeping wide of the lectern, and take the hollowed stair. The cloister is empty apart from the sundial and its long shadow. At the end of the east walk a short passage runs to the cellarer's low door. The old bean-row brother stands there at a stone trough, scrubbing out his clay pot with a handful of straw. When you ask to be let out by the garden, he nods at the latch without stopping.

"Lift and pull. Then drop it again behind you. He counts that latch, the cellarer." He thinks about it. "Not really. But he'd notice."

You lift it, pull, and drop it behind you the way you found it. You go down the gravel between the bean poles, where the shadows now stripe the whole path, pull the wicket's string, and go out. The gate claps shut behind you.

You cross the lane at a townsman's pace and walk into the gap between the woodstores like a man taking a shortcut home.

It's the footway. You know it a few yards in. The back walls of the main-street houses rise on your right and ivy-grown yard walls run along your left. There's barely a shield's width between them the whole way. Two people can't pass anywhere without one turning sideways, and a man carrying something in both arms would fill it. For the first hundred feet or so the backs are sheds and a woodstore. There are no gates, only one privy door hanging open on a broken strap. Then come kitchen doors and a slop-drain. A back step has a crust of bread trodden into the dirt below it, and the door above it is shut. Behind it a forge roars as the bellows go. Two houses further on, the right-hand wall rises.

It's ten feet of limewashed stone with broken crockery along the top, just as you saw it at one o'clock from the other end. You stop twenty feet short, put a boot up on a mounting stone that serves some kitchen door, and work at a lace.

The iron-studded door sits flush in the wall. Nothing about it says anyone uses it. A cobweb runs across the crack between the door and the stone at shoulder height, unbroken and grey with dust, not new. The dirt at the sill is the same as the dirt everywhere else in the footway. There's no worn track, no scuff and no swept arc where a door has swung out. Rust has run from the lowest stud down the limewash in a brown streak that nobody has scrubbed off. Whatever goes in and out of Thole's goes by the front. The shutter above is closed. Cool air breathes from the barred vent near your boots, the same as before, and there's no sound in it.

You look both ways along the footway. A woman further up toward the cooper's end is tipping a pail into the drain. She goes back in without looking your way. There's no thin man, and no lanky boy coming back with his basket. Nobody is anywhere they have no reason to be.

You finish the lace, turn round, and walk it back at the same pace, counting as you go. From Thole's wall past the forge step and the sheds to the woodstore gap, then across the lane to the wicket, it's a little under three hundred paces. That's about five minutes for a man walking without hurrying. It would take longer with something heavy to carry and somebody slower behind you.

The wicket's string hangs where it did. Over the wall the bean rows are empty, and up on the east walk the archive window is still propped open a hand's width. It's about twenty to five.

Where you are: outside the priory garden wicket, on the lane · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

You pull the wicket's string, and the gate claps shut behind you. You go up the gravel between the bean poles, where the shadows now stripe the whole path. At the cellarer's low door you lift the latch, slip through, and drop it back into its keeper the way you found it.

The old brother is still at the stone trough at the end of the passage. He's finished with the pot and is rinsing dirt out of his knuckles one finger at a time. You nod to him on the way past.

"Latch is down. He'll count it right."

The brother shakes the water off his hands. "He'll count it wrong anyway. He always finds one more than there is." He says it without any malice and goes back to his fingers.

The cloister is empty. The sundial's shadow is a long finger across the grass now. You climb the hollowed stair and knock once with a knuckle beside the bell-pull. After a moment the bolt draws, and Sister Maudra stands in the gap with her spectacles pushed up on her forehead and a finger still holding her place in the roll-book.

She hears you out in the doorway. She doesn't interrupt the paces or the cobweb, and she doesn't interrupt the rust streak down the limewash. At *a hundred feet in the open* she lets the spectacles drop onto her nose.

"I walked that footway at fifteen. It hasn't got any wider." She steps back to let you in. "Then whoever carries it doesn't stop to talk to anybody on the main street. Not a neighbour, and not a man on a bench who calls out good day." That's the whole of her advice. She goes back down the long room to her end of the table, sits, and finds her line again.

You take your place at the end window, a pace back in the sill's shadow, with the prop left as it was.

Below you the bean rows are empty. The wicket's string hangs still. While you watch, the lanky forge boy comes out of the woodstore gap again with his empty basket on his hip. He heaps it from the cut-wood stacks, gets it onto his shoulder, and goes back into the footway the way he came, as unhurried as before. After that there's only the cat, who has given up on the sun and gone somewhere else. The shadow of the sheds has climbed halfway up the garden wall. Nobody stops at the wicket, nobody lingers at the mouth of the gap, and behind you Maudra turns a page about once a minute.

It's about ten to five. Nothing else happens at this window before the bell unless you want it to.

*(Out of game: as agreed, everything in your thread after 13:50 still waits to be rewritten. Once the others pick their next move at 13:58, this scene may change to fit it. None of your four actions needed a roll, since each was routine with nothing uncertain riding on it.)*

Where you are: at the end window of Sister Maudra's long room, overlooking the garden · Time: Day 1 · afternoon

Under the retcon, you were never in the archive. At ten to two you left Teo's table, walked the shaded strip along the chapter house wall and turned the corner at the buttress into the east lane. You have been at the garden wicket about ten minutes.

The lane is quiet in the early afternoon. Over the wall the bean poles stand in their tied pairs, and the brother in the straw hat is bent over the far rows with his back to the cloister. Across the lane, between two woodstores, is the narrow mouth of a path. From the ground you can't see where it goes. A cat sits on the shed roofs and watches you.

You lean on the wall beside the latch-string and check your kit by touch, without looking down. The shortsword sits loose in its scabbard. Both daggers are where your hand expects them. In the satchel you turn the stoppers of the three red flasks outward so your fingers find them without fumbling. The bow stays unstrung on your back.

Then you hear iron rings shifting on a man who walks, coming from the square end of the lane. It's an unhurried, heavy step. A brown-painted shield comes round the buttress into the lane, and two paces behind it, keeping to the shade, comes a woman in dark leather. It's a few minutes past two.

*(Out of game: as agreed, your afternoon after 1:50 is replaced. The archive, Maudra, the second talk with Lucan and the footway walk never happened, so you know only what you had by 1:50. The three of you are now together at the wicket, and Bram's words are spoken next round.)*

*(Out of game: no roll was needed, because nothing was uncertain. You checked your kit by touch, and under the retcon you wait at the garden wicket rather than the archive window.)*

Where you are: garden wicket, east lane · Time: Day 1 · evening

Bram rounds the buttress with Sefa behind him, and you come off the garden wall to meet them halfway down the lane. The three of you stop in the shed's shadow with the corner of the temple between you and the square. The plank wicket is a few steps behind you. Across the ruts is the gap between the two woodstores. From down here it's only a dark slot between stacked logs.

Bram stops where he leaves the lane clear and keeps his voice under the hum of the bees.

"We looked for you at noon. Glad you're on your feet. We've got Aubrey's ticket and the court's sealed ruling. Hesper has the redemption money ready at home."

He glances back toward the corner, then turns to you. "What did you find—and what's this cart we need to catch?"

Sefa comes up at the same even pace without raising a hand. Her eyes go to the coal grit on your knees and the tar on your coat before they go to your face. She stops close enough to speak low.

"Pell. You've been down, then up. Tell us where—and what cart you meant. We have the day by the throat, but we've been bright about it, not quiet."

She glances once over her shoulder toward the square, then back. "Bram has a sealed ruling from the temple, and I'm carrying the ticket itself. Sister Maudra found it for us. So if that cart can wait, we go to Hesper's now; if it can't, we hear about it before we step back out in front of any man on a bench."

You give it to them short and low: the bench and what the big man on it can see, the stable lad at the Red Sheaf and the man in the grey riding cloak, the chandler's slate and *Ashby & Corve*, the two hired swords, the lamp oil and the new tinderbox. You say nothing about the cart. Then you put your own questions to them, one after another.

Over the wall the old brother in the straw hat has straightened up between two bean poles. He watches the three of you muttering beside his gate the way a man watches weather coming. Nobody looks back at him. After a moment he sniffs, bends again and goes on pinching blackfly into his clay pot.

Nobody else is in the lane. The cat on the shed roofs has its eyes shut. From the square round the corner comes the sound of the fountain, and nothing else. It's a few minutes past two, and you're waiting for answers.

*(Out of game: this was honest talk, so no roll. You gave your whole report, then asked whether they came by the steps or along the wall, whether the court gave the writing, what Maudra wanted and how long the warden keeps hearing. Those questions are put to Bram and Sefa, so the turn stops there for their answers.)*

Where you are: shed's shadow, lane behind the temple · Time: Day 1 · evening
